ELA.overview: Teach about 60–90 minutes a day: read the named book aloud or together, then practice phonics, grammar, and writing tied to it. Always preview the day's text first so you can ask the questions with confidence, and ask the child to point to the words or pictures that prove each answer. Keep a reading log all year, reread favorite stories for fluency, and use the Friday checks to choose which spelling patterns to review.

weeks.prep: Get Frog and Toad Are Friends (Arnold Lobel) and read 'Spring' and 'The Story' yourself first. Make a reading log (date, title, pages), 12 short-a/short-i word cards (cap, cab, map, ham, bag, pin, fit, sit, big, lip, tap, rib), a whiteboard, and a 10-word spelling list.
misconceptions: Writing sentences that are fragments ('Frog and Toad.'). Ask 'Who or what? What did they do?' — both parts are needed: 'Frog and Toad went for a walk.'
Answering comprehension questions from memory or imagination instead of the text. Ask 'Where in the story did it say that?' and flip back to find the page.

days.guide: Hold up the book and read 'Spring' aloud, pausing to let the child look at the pictures. Ask who, what, and where questions, then the child draws the setting. Start the reading log together and practice 'listen, then add on' ('I agree, and also…').

questions.q: In 'Spring,' what did Frog want Toad to do?
questions.a: Wake up and come outside, because spring had come.

questions.q: How did Frog get Toad to get up?
questions.a: Toad said to wake him at half past May, so Frog tore the calendar pages (November through April) off until it showed May.

days.guide: Blend short-a and short-i words sound by sound (c-a-p, cap) and sort 12 cards into short a / short i columns. The child rereads 'Spring' aloud to you; then writes 2 sentences about what Frog wanted.

questions.q: Sort: cap, pin, cab, fit. Which have short a?
questions.a: cap and cab (short a); pin and fit have short i.

questions.q: Write a sentence telling what Frog wanted in 'Spring.'
questions.a: Model: Frog wanted Toad to wake up and play with him in the spring.

days.guide: Show a sentence: capital at the start, end mark at the end, and a whole idea. Fix 6 scrambled sentences together ('went Toad home' → 'Toad went home.'). Read 'The Story' and ask why/how questions.

questions.q: In 'The Story,' why does Toad try to think of a story?
questions.a: Frog is not feeling well, and he asks Toad to tell him a story.

questions.q: How does Toad try to think of a story?
questions.a: He walks up and down the porch, stands on his head, pours water over his head, and bangs his head against the wall — but he can't think of one. Then Frog tells a story about what Toad just did.

days.guide: Partner talk: the child describes Toad with two words (e.g., kind, silly) and points to a picture or sentence that proves each. Then the child writes 3 complete sentences about a friend.

questions.q: Give one word that describes Toad in 'The Story' and your evidence.
questions.a: Example: caring — he tries very hard to tell Frog a story because Frog is sick; or silly — he pours water on his head to get an idea.

questions.q: Is 'my friend Sam' a complete sentence? Fix it.
questions.a: No. Example: My friend Sam likes to play tag.

days.guide: Give the 10-word spelling check. Time the child reading one page for one minute and note words read correctly. Ask 3 oral comprehension questions and record the books read this week in the log.

questions.q: Where does 'Spring' take place?
questions.a: At Toad's house (Frog comes over to wake him).

questions.q: Spell 'pin' and 'map.'
questions.a: p-i-n; m-a-p.

weeks.assessment_key: Spelling (suggested 10): cap, map, bag, ham, tap, pin, fit, sit, big, lip — score out of 10 (8+ proficient). Oral who/what/where (on 'Spring'): Who? Frog and Toad. What happened? Frog tried to wake Toad up because spring had come; Toad wanted to sleep until May, so Frog tore pages off the calendar until it said May. Where? At Toad's house. Journal sentences: proficient = 3 sentences, each a whole idea with a capital letter and end punctuation.

weeks.prep: Preview 'A Lost Button' and 'A Swim' in Frog and Toad Are Friends. Gather sticky notes, drawing paper, a problem/solution chart, and short o/u/e word cards (hop, lot, pond, bug, cup, bed, net, sun, hen, fox).
misconceptions: Retelling every tiny detail or retelling out of order. Use first, next, then, last on fingers — one event per finger.
Calling verbs or describing words nouns. Ask 'Can you see it or touch it, or is it a person or place?' — those are nouns.

days.guide: Read 'A Lost Button.' Each time a button is found, the child writes it on a sticky note (black, two holes, small, thin, square). Ask how Toad feels each time. Then read short-o words.

questions.q: Why did Toad keep saying 'That is not my button'?
questions.a: Each button was wrong: his button was white, with four holes, big, round, and thick.

questions.q: How did Toad feel as each wrong button was found?
questions.a: More and more upset and angry — he finally shouts and runs home.

days.guide: Fill a problem/solution chart together. Ask how Toad makes things right at the end. Then sort short-u and short-e words.

questions.q: What is the problem in 'A Lost Button'?
questions.a: Toad lost a button from his jacket.

questions.q: How does Toad fix things at the end?
questions.a: He finds his button on his floor, sews all the buttons onto his jacket, and gives it to Frog as a present.

days.guide: Teach: a noun names a person, place, or thing. Circle the nouns in 8 sentences from the story, then list 10 nouns at home. Read 'A Swim' with expression (Toad's lines sound embarrassed).

questions.q: Circle the nouns: 'Toad lost a button on the path.'
questions.a: Toad, button, path.

questions.q: In 'A Swim,' why doesn't Toad want anyone to see him?
questions.a: He thinks he looks funny in his bathing suit.

days.guide: Brainstorm 3 small moments (one short event, like losing a tooth), pick one, and sketch it in 3 boxes. The child tells the story aloud with details.

questions.q: Which is a small moment: 'my summer' or 'the time I caught a frog'?
questions.a: The time I caught a frog — one short event.

questions.q: What goes in the three boxes?
questions.a: The beginning, middle, and end of the moment.

days.guide: Give the spelling check. The child retells 'A Lost Button' using first, next, then, last, and writes one sentence about how Toad changed (angry → generous).

questions.q: How did Toad change in 'A Lost Button'?
questions.a: He went from angry and upset to sorry and generous — he gave Frog a jacket with all the buttons.

questions.q: Spell 'pond' and 'bug.'
questions.a: p-o-n-d; b-u-g.

weeks.assessment_key: Problem/solution chart: Problem — Toad lost a button from his jacket. Attempts — Frog and Toad search and find wrong buttons (black, two holes, small, thin, square; Toad's was white, four holes, big, thick, round). Solution — Toad finds his button on his floor at home, sews all the found buttons on his jacket, and gives it to Frog. Spelling (suggested): hop, lot, pond, bug, cup, sun, bed, net, hen, pet (8+ proficient). Retell: correct order (lost the button → searched and found wrong buttons → Toad got angry and went home → found it on his floor → sewed the buttons on the jacket and gave it to Frog).

weeks.prep: Get Frog and Toad Together and preview 'A List,' 'Cookies,' and 'The Garden.' Make digraph cards (sh, ch, th, wh, ck) and a collective-noun matching set (flock/birds, herd/cows, team/players, class/students, school/fish, pack/wolves, bunch/grapes, swarm/bees).
misconceptions: Reading digraphs as two sounds (s-h in 'ship'). Teach that two letters can make one new sound and practice with picture cards.
Story drafts with 'and then… and then…' Replace with temporal words: first, next, after that, finally.

days.guide: Read 'A List.' Make the child's own to-do list for the day. Teach sh, ch, th: read and write ship, chop, thin, wish, much, bath.

questions.q: In 'A List,' why doesn't Toad chase his list when the wind blows it away?
questions.a: Running after the list was not one of the things written on his list.

questions.q: How does Toad end his day?
questions.a: He writes 'Go to sleep' on the ground with a stick, crosses it out, and goes to sleep.

days.guide: Read 'Cookies' and ask why they can't stop eating and how they try to stop. Explain 'willpower.' Build a wh/ck word ladder (when → whip; duck → sock).

questions.q: Why can't Frog and Toad stop eating the cookies?
questions.a: The cookies are very good, and they keep wanting just one more.

questions.q: How do they try to solve the problem, and what finally happens?
questions.a: They put the cookies in a box, tie it with string, and put it on a high shelf, but they could still open it; Frog gives the cookies to the birds. Toad goes home to bake a cake.

days.guide: Teach collective nouns (a flock of birds, a herd of cows). Match pairs and write 4 sentences. Read 'The Garden' aloud with a partner, taking turns by page.

questions.q: What do we call a group of cows? Of students?
questions.a: A herd of cows; a class of students.

questions.q: In 'The Garden,' what does Toad do to make his seeds grow?
questions.a: He shouts at them, reads them stories, sings songs, reads poems, and plays music. They grow after he falls asleep — really, seeds just need time, sun, and rain.

days.guide: Draft the small moment using first, next, then, after that, finally. Prompt for senses: 'What did you see? Hear? Feel?'

questions.q: Name 3 temporal words.
questions.a: first, next, then, after that, finally (any 3).

questions.q: Add a feeling to: 'I jumped in the pool.'
questions.a: Example: I jumped in the pool and the cold water made me shiver.

days.guide: Give the spelling check and the collective-noun quiz. The child reads the draft aloud to a family member, who asks one question.

questions.q: Spell 'wish' and 'duck.'
questions.a: w-i-s-h; d-u-c-k.

questions.q: What is a group of fish called?
questions.a: A school of fish.

weeks.assessment_key: Spelling (suggested 10): ship, chop, thin, wish, much, bath, when, duck, sock, whip. Collective nouns (8): flock of birds, herd of cows, team of players, class of students, school of fish, pack of wolves, bunch of grapes, swarm of bees. Narrative draft: proficient = tells one small moment in order with at least 3 temporal words and at least one detail of what the child saw, heard, or felt.

weeks.prep: Get Henry and Mudge: The First Book (Cynthia Rylant) and preview it. Gather colored pencils, letter tiles for blends, a revision checklist (2 details, feeling sentence, capitals, end marks), and set up an 'author's chair.' For Friday, pick a Frog and Toad story the child hasn't read (e.g., 'The Letter' or 'Alone').
misconceptions: Dropping a sound in blends (reading 'stop' as 'sop'). Tap each sound: /s/ /t/ /o/ /p/.
Thinking revising means recopying neatly. Revising = adding or changing ideas; editing = fixing capitals, spelling, and punctuation.

days.guide: Read chapters 1–2. Ask how Henry feels before he gets Mudge and after. Read initial-blend words (bl, cr, st, fl).

questions.q: How does Henry feel before he gets Mudge, and why?
questions.a: Lonely — he has no brothers or sisters and there are no children on his street.

questions.q: How does Mudge change after Henry gets him?
questions.a: Mudge grows and grows into a huge dog (180 pounds) — and Henry isn't lonely anymore.

days.guide: Read chapter 3. Discuss how Henry and Mudge each feel and act when Mudge gets lost. Build final-blend words (-nd, -st, -mp) with tiles.

questions.q: How do Henry and Mudge feel when Mudge is lost?
questions.a: Both feel scared and sad; Mudge misses Henry and Henry misses Mudge.

questions.q: Build a word ending in -mp.
questions.a: Examples: jump, camp, lamp, stamp.

days.guide: Reread the draft and add 2 details and a feeling sentence in colored pencil. Then edit with the checklist for capitals and end marks.

questions.q: Add a feeling sentence to 'We went to the beach.'
questions.a: Example: My heart was pounding when the big wave came.

questions.q: What is the difference between revising and editing?
questions.a: Revising changes ideas (adding details); editing fixes capitals, spelling, and punctuation.

days.guide: The child copies the revised story neatly, illustrates each part, and adds a title. Practice reading it aloud at a steady pace.

questions.q: What should a good title do?
questions.a: Tell what the story is about and make people want to read it.

questions.q: How should you read your story aloud?
questions.a: At a steady pace, loud enough, with expression.

days.guide: Author's chair: the child reads the narrative to family and answers questions. Then give the 12-word spelling check and the story-element quiz on a new Frog and Toad story.

questions.q: Name the story elements.
questions.a: Characters, setting, problem, events, and solution.

questions.q: In 'The Letter,' what is Toad's problem?
questions.a: He is sad because he never gets any mail.

weeks.assessment_key: Narrative rubric (4 = proficient-plus, 3 = proficient): Sequence — events in clear order with temporal words; Details — at least 2 details and a feeling; Closing — a sentence that wraps up the moment; Conventions — capitals and end marks mostly correct. Spelling (suggested 12): black, crab, stop, flag, frog, sled, hand, best, jump, ship, chin, thank. Story-element quiz on the new Frog and Toad story: characters (Frog, Toad), setting, problem, and solution named correctly (e.g., 'The Letter': Toad is sad because he never gets mail; Frog writes him a letter and a snail delivers it four days later).

weeks.prep: Find Aesop's Fables (Project Gutenberg or library) and preview 'The Lion and the Mouse,' 'The Tortoise and the Hare,' and 'The Fox and the Grapes.' Make 4 sequence cards for 'The Lion and the Mouse' and CVC/CVCe word cards (cap/cape, kit/kite, hop/hope, cub/cube, tap/tape).
misconceptions: Thinking the moral is a plot summary ('The tortoise won'). A moral is the lesson for people: 'Slow and steady wins the race.'
Forgetting the silent e changes the vowel. Show that magic e makes the vowel say its name: cap → cape.

days.guide: Read 'The Lion and the Mouse' aloud. The child orders 4 sequence cards and retells. Discuss the moral.

questions.q: Why does the lion let the mouse go?
questions.a: The mouse promises to help him someday, and the lion is amused and lets him go.

questions.q: How does the mouse help the lion later?
questions.a: The lion is caught in a hunter's net, and the mouse gnaws the ropes to free him.

days.guide: Show cap → cape: adding e makes the a say its name. Read 20 CVCe words and write 3 sentences with them.

questions.q: What word do you make when you add e to 'kit'?
questions.a: kite.

questions.q: Read: hop, hope. What changed?
questions.a: Adding e makes the o long: hope.

days.guide: Read 'The Tortoise and the Hare.' Compare how each acts in the race and write the moral in your own words.

questions.q: Why does the hare lose the race?
questions.a: He is so sure he will win that he stops to nap, and the tortoise keeps going and passes him.

questions.q: What does 'slow and steady wins the race' mean?
questions.a: If you keep working and don't give up, you can succeed, even if you aren't the fastest.

days.guide: Teach: names of people, pets, and places start with capitals. Fix 8 sentences. The child retells a fable with first, next, then, last.

questions.q: Fix: 'my dog rex lives in ohio.'
questions.a: My dog Rex lives in Ohio.

questions.q: Which words need capitals: 'aesop told a fable about a lion'?
questions.a: Aesop (a person's name) and the first word, so: 'Aesop told a fable about a lion.'

days.guide: Give the CVCe spelling check, match 4 fables to their morals, and have the child read 'The Fox and the Grapes' alone and write its lesson.

questions.q: In 'The Fox and the Grapes,' what does the fox say when he can't reach the grapes?
questions.a: That the grapes are probably sour anyway.

questions.q: What is the lesson?
questions.a: People sometimes say they don't want what they can't have.

weeks.assessment_key: Fable-moral matching: 'The Lion and the Mouse' → little friends can be great friends (kindness is repaid); 'The Tortoise and the Hare' → slow and steady wins the race; 'The Fox and the Grapes' → it is easy to dislike what you cannot have ('sour grapes'); 'The Boy Who Cried Wolf' → no one believes a liar, even when he tells the truth. Written moral for 'The Fox and the Grapes': proficient states the lesson in a sentence (e.g., 'People sometimes pretend they didn't want something they couldn't get'). CVCe spelling (suggested): cape, kite, hope, cube, tape, bike, home, cake, rope, mule.

weeks.prep: Preview 'The Ant and the Grasshopper,' 'The Crow and the Pitcher,' and 'The Boy Who Cried Wolf.' Gather a tall cup, water, and pebbles; vowel-team cards (ai, ay, ee, ea); and picture cards for irregular plurals.
misconceptions: Adding -s to every plural (foots, childs, mouses). Make a chart of 'special plurals' and practice them orally.
Spelling long a with ay in the middle of a word (trayn). Teach: ai in the middle, ay at the end.

days.guide: Read 'The Ant and the Grasshopper.' Chart what each does in summer and winter. Read ai/ay words.

questions.q: What do the ant and grasshopper do in summer?
questions.a: The ant works storing food; the grasshopper sings and plays.

questions.q: What happens in winter, and what is the lesson?
questions.a: The grasshopper has no food and is hungry while the ant has plenty. Lesson: work and prepare ahead for what you will need.

days.guide: Read 'The Crow and the Pitcher,' then test it: drop pebbles into a cup of water and watch the water rise. Read ee/ea words.

questions.q: How does the crow get a drink?
questions.a: It drops pebbles into the pitcher one by one until the water rises high enough to drink.

questions.q: What is the lesson?
questions.a: Little by little does the trick — thinking and keeping at it can solve a problem.

days.guide: Teach plurals that change: foot/feet, child/children, tooth/teeth, mouse/mice, fish/fish. Complete 10 sentences. Practice answering 'What is the lesson?' in a complete sentence.

questions.q: What is the plural of mouse? Of tooth?
questions.a: mice; teeth.

questions.q: Complete: Two ___ (child) played.
questions.a: children.

days.guide: The child writes 3–4 sentences about a time a moral came true in their life and draws a picture.

questions.q: Which moral fits saving allowance for a toy?
questions.a: The Ant and the Grasshopper — work and save ahead.

questions.q: What should the last sentence do?
questions.a: Tell how the moral came true or what was learned.

days.guide: Give the spelling check and plural quiz. The child reads 'The Boy Who Cried Wolf' aloud and tells the moral.

questions.q: Why didn't the villagers come when the wolf really came?
questions.a: The boy had lied about a wolf before, so they didn't believe him.

questions.q: Spell 'train' and 'beach.'
questions.a: t-r-a-i-n; b-e-a-c-h.

weeks.assessment_key: Spelling (suggested 12): rain, train, wait, play, day, stay, tree, green, feet, beach, read, team. Irregular plural quiz (10): foot/feet, child/children, tooth/teeth, mouse/mice, fish/fish, man/men, woman/women, goose/geese, sheep/sheep, person/people. Fable-to-life connection rubric: 3 = names a moral and tells a real event where it came true, 3–4 sentences; 2 = event without clear link to the moral; 1 = off topic. 'The Boy Who Cried Wolf' moral: if you lie, people won't believe you even when you tell the truth.

weeks.prep: Get The Little Red Hen (any version) and Stone Soup (Marcia Brown or Jon J Muth). Gather paper bags, markers, and glue for puppets, and long-o/long-i word cards (boat, snow, toe, night, pie, fly).
misconceptions: Reading dialogue in the same flat voice. Point to quotation marks and ask 'Who is talking? How would they sound?'
Writing the lesson as a plot event. The central message is what the story teaches: 'Sharing makes everyone better off.'

days.guide: Read The Little Red Hen. Ask why the hen would not share the bread and whether it was fair. Read oa/ow/oe words.

questions.q: Who helped the Little Red Hen plant, cut, and bake the wheat?
questions.a: No one — the dog, cat, and duck each said 'Not I,' so she did it all herself.

questions.q: Why didn't the hen share the bread?
questions.a: The others refused to help with any of the work, so she ate it herself (with her chicks).

days.guide: Read Stone Soup. Compare its lesson about sharing with the hen's story. Play a sentence-building game with igh/ie/y words.

questions.q: How do the travelers get the villagers to share food?
questions.a: They say they will make soup from stones; then they suggest the soup would be even better with a carrot or cabbage, and each villager adds something until there is a feast.

questions.q: How are the lessons of The Little Red Hen and Stone Soup different?
questions.a: The Hen teaches that people who don't help don't share the reward; Stone Soup teaches that when everyone shares a little, everyone has plenty.

days.guide: Read the hen's story dialogue using a different voice for the hen, dog, cat, and duck. Make paper-bag puppets.

questions.q: How might the hen's voice sound at the end?
questions.a: Firm or proud: 'Then I will eat it myself!'

questions.q: What do quotation marks tell a reader?
questions.a: Which words a character says out loud.

days.guide: The child writes a 5-sentence retelling of Stone Soup with beginning, middle, end, and the lesson last, then underlines time-order words.

questions.q: What happens at the beginning of Stone Soup?
questions.a: Hungry travelers come to a village where people hide their food.

questions.q: Write the lesson as a last sentence.
questions.a: Example: When everyone shared a little, there was a feast for all.

days.guide: Perform The Little Red Hen puppet show. Give the 12-word spelling check and ask the child to write the central message.

questions.q: What is the central message of The Little Red Hen?
questions.a: If you don't help with the work, you shouldn't expect to share the reward.

questions.q: Spell 'night' and 'boat.'
questions.a: n-i-g-h-t; b-o-a-t.

weeks.assessment_key: Puppet show rubric: 3 = different voices for hen, dog, cat, and duck, reads fluently with few errors; 2 = some voice changes, some hesitations; 1 = flat or many errors. Spelling (suggested 12): boat, coat, road, snow, grow, toe, night, light, pie, tie, fly, sky. Central message: The Little Red Hen — those who don't help with the work shouldn't expect to share the reward; Stone Soup — when everyone shares a little, there is plenty for all.

weeks.prep: Get Anansi and the Moss-Covered Rock (Eric A. Kimmel) and preview it. Make a fable planning sheet (characters, traits, problem, ending, moral) and a short reader's theater script of 'The Lion and the Mouse' (Narrator, Lion, Mouse, Hunters). For Friday, pick a short folktale the child hasn't read.
misconceptions: Writing a fable with no lesson. Have the child decide the moral first, then plan a story that teaches it.
Forgetting quotation marks around dialogue. Highlight the exact words spoken and put marks around them.

days.guide: Read Anansi and the Moss-Covered Rock (West African). Discuss Anansi's trick and how Little Bush Deer turns it around. Notice how the beginning introduces the trick and the ending wraps it up.

questions.q: What is Anansi's trick?
questions.a: Anyone who says 'Isn't this a strange moss-covered rock!' falls down asleep, so Anansi brings animals to the rock and steals their food while they are knocked out.

questions.q: How does Little Bush Deer teach Anansi a lesson?
questions.a: She tricks Anansi into saying the magic words himself, so he falls asleep, and the animals take back their food.

days.guide: Pick two animals with opposite traits (e.g., a boastful rabbit and a patient snail) and a lesson. Fill in the fable organizer. Hunt for vowel-team words in the Anansi book.

questions.q: What should you decide first when planning a fable?
questions.a: The lesson (moral) the story will teach.

questions.q: Why give the characters opposite traits?
questions.a: So the difference causes the problem and shows the lesson.

days.guide: Draft the fable with dialogue and a moral as the last line. Read it to a listener and ask 'Was my lesson clear?'

questions.q: Where does the moral go in a fable?
questions.a: At the end, usually as the last line.

questions.q: Punctuate: Hurry up said the rabbit
questions.a: "Hurry up," said the rabbit.

days.guide: Edit with a checklist and publish with illustrations. Rehearse 'The Lion and the Mouse' reader's theater with expression.

questions.q: What does the mouse say when the lion catches him?
questions.a: He begs to be let go and promises to help the lion someday.

questions.q: Name 2 things on the editing checklist.
questions.a: Capitals, end marks, spelling of vowel-team words.

days.guide: Perform the reader's theater and read the fable aloud. Give the unit test on a new folktale: moral, sequence of 4 events, and 12 spelling words.

questions.q: What is a moral?
questions.a: The lesson a story teaches.

questions.q: Spell 'team' and 'grow.'
questions.a: t-e-a-m; g-r-o-w.

weeks.assessment_key: Original fable rubric (3 = proficient): Characters — two animals with opposite traits; Problem — clear problem caused by a trait; Moral — stated as the last line and matches the story; Conventions — capitals, end marks, vowel-team spelling mostly correct. Unit test on a cold-read folktale: moral written in one sentence that fits the story; 4 events sequenced correctly; spelling (suggested 12): rain, play, tree, beach, boat, snow, toe, night, pie, fly, team, grow.

weeks.prep: Get National Geographic Readers: Frogs! (Elizabeth Carney) or another NatGeo Kids reader, plus 10 mixed library books, sticky flags, and a magnifying glass. Print a short ReadWorks animal passage with headings for Friday and write 6 text-feature questions.
misconceptions: Thinking fiction is anything with pictures. Fiction is made up; nonfiction gives true facts — check for headings, photos, captions, and a glossary.
Reading the whole book to find one fact. Teach jumping to the table of contents or index first.

days.guide: Sort 10 books into fiction and nonfiction, saying the clue for each. Tour Frogs! and flag a heading, caption, bold word, and the glossary.

questions.q: Is Frogs! fiction or nonfiction? How do you know?
questions.a: Nonfiction — it gives true facts with real photos, headings, captions, and a glossary.

questions.q: What does a caption do?
questions.a: It tells about a picture or photo.

days.guide: Use the table of contents and index to answer 5 questions from Frogs!. Read ar words.

questions.q: Where do you look to find which page tells what frogs eat?
questions.a: The index (look up 'food' or 'eat') or the table of contents.

questions.q: What is the difference between the table of contents and the index?
questions.a: The table of contents is at the front and lists chapters in order; the index is at the back and lists topics in ABC order with page numbers.

days.guide: Look up 5 bold words in the glossary and draw each. Sort or words.

questions.q: Why are some words in bold print?
questions.a: They are important words; their meanings are in the glossary.

questions.q: Frogs are amphibians. What does that mean?
questions.a: Animals that live part of their lives in water and part on land (frogs start as tadpoles in water).

days.guide: Sort words from Frogs! into nouns and verbs (frog, leap, pond, swim). Write 4 fact sentences, each with a noun and verb.

questions.q: Sort: frog, leap, pond, swim.
questions.a: Nouns: frog, pond. Verbs: leap, swim.

questions.q: Write a fact sentence about frogs with a noun and a verb.
questions.a: Example: Frogs catch insects with their sticky tongues.

days.guide: Have the child use text features to answer 6 questions on a new animal passage, then give the ar/or spelling check.

questions.q: Which feature helps you find a section quickly?
questions.a: A heading (or the table of contents).

questions.q: Spell 'storm' and 'farm.'
questions.a: s-t-o-r-m; f-a-r-m.

weeks.assessment_key: Text-feature hunt on the new passage: answers depend on the passage — check that the child uses the correct feature (heading to find a section, caption to explain a photo, bold word + glossary for meanings, table of contents for page numbers). 6/6 or 5/6 = proficient. Spelling (suggested 10): car, farm, star, park, hard, corn, storm, horse, fork, short.

weeks.prep: Get Monarch Butterfly (Gail Gibbons) and preview it, especially the migration pages. Gather paper plates, brads, crayons, a note-taking sheet, and an er/ir/ur word list. Print a ReadWorks butterfly passage with 4 questions for Friday.
misconceptions: Thinking caterpillars and butterflies are different animals. Show the life-cycle wheel: the caterpillar (larva) becomes the butterfly.
Copying whole sentences as notes. Model writing 2–4 key words: 'eats milkweed.'

days.guide: Read Monarch Butterfly and list the 4 stages. Teach that er, ir, ur make the same sound.

questions.q: What are the 4 stages of a monarch's life?
questions.a: Egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa (chrysalis), adult.

questions.q: What plant do monarch caterpillars eat?
questions.a: Milkweed.

days.guide: Make a paper-plate life-cycle wheel. The child explains each step using 'because' and 'then.' Use context to define larva and chrysalis.

questions.q: What is a chrysalis?
questions.a: The hard case a monarch caterpillar forms around itself while it changes into a butterfly (the pupa stage).

questions.q: Explain how one stage leads to the next.
questions.a: The egg hatches into a caterpillar, then the caterpillar eats and grows, then it makes a chrysalis, then a butterfly comes out and lays eggs.

days.guide: Model taking notes in a few words. The child records 6 monarch facts. Sort er/ir/ur words.

questions.q: Turn this into a note: 'The caterpillar eats milkweed leaves all day long.'
questions.a: eats milkweed leaves.

questions.q: Sort: bird, her, turn.
questions.a: ir: bird; er: her; ur: turn.

days.guide: Read the migration section. The child writes why monarchs fly to California and Mexico using notes, then asks a partner a clarifying question.

questions.q: Why do monarchs fly to California and Mexico?
questions.a: To escape the cold winter — they cannot survive freezing weather, so they fly to warmer places.

questions.q: What is a clarifying question?
questions.a: A question that asks someone to explain more, e.g., 'What do you mean by…?'

days.guide: The child draws and labels the life cycle, takes the spelling check, and answers 4 questions on a butterfly passage.

questions.q: What comes after the larva stage?
questions.a: The pupa (chrysalis) stage.

questions.q: Spell 'bird' and 'turn.'
questions.a: b-i-r-d; t-u-r-n.

weeks.assessment_key: Life-cycle drawing: 4 stages labeled in order — egg → larva (caterpillar) → pupa (chrysalis) → adult butterfly — with arrows back to egg. Migration answer: proficient says monarchs fly south to warmer places (Mexico and the California coast) in fall because they cannot survive the cold winter up north, using at least one fact from notes. Spelling (suggested 10): her, fern, bird, girl, first, turn, burn, hurt, nurse, shirt.

weeks.prep: Get From Tadpole to Frog (Wendy Pfeffer) and 2 library books about an animal the child chooses. Prepare a 3-box note sheet (body, home, food) and a y-word list (happy, funny, baby, sky, fly, cry, my, puppy). Print a new 3-paragraph passage for Friday.
misconceptions: Confusing the main topic with one detail ('frogs have long legs'). Ask 'What is the WHOLE book mostly about?'
Writing a paragraph without a topic sentence. The first sentence should tell what the whole paragraph is about.

days.guide: Read From Tadpole to Frog and name the main topic. Reread 3 paragraphs; the child tells what each is mostly about. Teach y as long e (happy) and long i (sky).

questions.q: What is From Tadpole to Frog mostly about?
questions.a: How a frog grows and changes from an egg to a tadpole to a grown frog.

questions.q: How does a tadpole breathe underwater?
questions.a: With gills, like a fish.

days.guide: Study the life-cycle diagram. Ask what it shows that the words don't (all stages at once, in order). The child draws a labeled tadpole.

questions.q: What does the diagram show that the words do not?
questions.a: All the stages side by side in order, so you can see how the body changes.

questions.q: In what order does a tadpole grow legs?
questions.a: Back legs first, then front legs; then the tail shrinks away.

days.guide: The child chooses an animal, reads 2 library books, and takes notes in 3 boxes: body, home, food.

questions.q: What 3 boxes do you use for notes?
questions.a: Body, home, and food.

questions.q: Why use 2 books instead of 1?
questions.a: To find more facts and check that facts match.

days.guide: Teach topic sentences. Draft paragraph 1 (body) with a topic sentence and 3 facts. Sort y words.

questions.q: Write a topic sentence for a paragraph about an owl's body.
questions.a: Example: Owls have bodies made for hunting at night.

questions.q: Sort: happy, sky.
questions.a: happy — y says long e; sky — y says long i.

days.guide: The child reads a new 3-paragraph passage and writes the main topic and focus of each paragraph, then takes the y-word spelling check.

questions.q: How do you find a paragraph's focus?
questions.a: Look at the first sentence and ask what most sentences are about.

questions.q: Spell 'puppy' and 'cry.'
questions.a: p-u-p-p-y; c-r-y.

weeks.assessment_key: Cold-read organizer: main topic stated correctly for the passage and one focus per paragraph (answers depend on the passage). First report paragraph rubric: 3 = topic sentence about the animal's body + 3 accurate facts in own words; 2 = facts but no topic sentence; 1 = fewer than 2 facts. Spelling (suggested): happy, funny, baby, puppy, sunny, sky, fly, cry, my, try.

weeks.prep: Have the child's animal notes, cardstock, markers, and Frogs!, Monarch Butterfly, and a Frog and Toad book on hand. Arrange a family audience or video call for Thursday. Prepare a cold-read nonfiction passage with questions for Friday.
misconceptions: Thinking every book's purpose is to entertain. Ask 'Did the author want to teach me, tell me a story, or convince me?'
Ending a report abruptly. Add a concluding sentence that sums up the animal.

days.guide: Compare purposes: Frogs! teaches facts; Frog and Toad entertains. Ask what question Monarch Butterfly answers. Finish report paragraph 2 (home).

questions.q: What is the author's purpose in Frogs!?
questions.a: To teach (inform) readers facts about frogs.

questions.q: What is the author's purpose in Frog and Toad Are Friends?
questions.a: To entertain readers with stories.

days.guide: Write paragraph 3 (food) and a concluding sentence. Add a labeled diagram and a 3-word glossary.

questions.q: Write a concluding sentence for a report on owls.
questions.a: Example: Owls are amazing night hunters.

questions.q: What goes in a glossary?
questions.a: Important words and what they mean, in ABC order.

days.guide: The child reads the report aloud, fixes anything that doesn't make sense, checks spelling, and makes a final copy on cardstock.

questions.q: Why read your writing aloud?
questions.a: To hear mistakes and parts that don't make sense.

questions.q: Spell 'shirt' and 'rain.'
questions.a: s-h-i-r-t; r-a-i-n.

days.guide: Present to family, speaking clearly. Listeners each ask one question; the child answers.

questions.q: What does a good presenter do?
questions.a: Speaks loud and clear, looks at the audience, and answers questions.

questions.q: Give an example of a question to gather more information.
questions.a: Example: 'What do baby owls eat?'

days.guide: Give the cold-read test (text features, main topic, author's purpose) and the 15-word spelling test.

questions.q: What is the author's purpose of a passage that explains how bees make honey?
questions.a: To teach/inform.

questions.q: Spell 'first' and 'storm.'
questions.a: f-i-r-s-t; s-t-o-r-m.

weeks.assessment_key: Report rubric (3 = proficient): topic sentence in each paragraph; at least 3 accurate facts per paragraph in the child's words; a labeled diagram; a concluding sentence; a 3-word glossary. Unit reading test: text features correctly used, main topic stated, author's purpose named (to teach/inform for a nonfiction passage). Spelling (suggested 15): bird, her, turn, first, burn, girl, nurse, farm, star, corn, storm, happy, baby, sky, fly.

weeks.prep: Get The Tale of Peter Rabbit and The Tale of Benjamin Bunny (Beatrix Potter, public domain) and preview both. Make a story map (characters, setting, beginning, problem, events, ending) and oi/oy word cards (coin, boy, soil, toy, oil, joy, point, enjoy).
misconceptions: Adding -ed to irregular verbs (runned, hided, eated). Make a T-chart of 'today / yesterday' verbs and say them in sentences.
Spelling oy in the middle of a word (boyl). Teach: oi in the middle, oy at the end.

days.guide: Read The Tale of Peter Rabbit and fill the story map. Discuss Mother's warning at the beginning. Read oi/oy words.

questions.q: What does Mrs. Rabbit warn her children at the beginning?
questions.a: Don't go into Mr. McGregor's garden — their father had an accident there and was put in a pie by Mrs. McGregor.

questions.q: What does Peter do instead?
questions.a: He goes straight into Mr. McGregor's garden and eats lettuces, French beans, and radishes.

days.guide: Reread. Describe how Peter responds when Mr. McGregor chases him, using illustrations as evidence. Write 3 sentences about his feelings.

questions.q: How does Peter try to escape?
questions.a: He runs, loses his shoes, gets caught in a gooseberry net by his jacket buttons, wriggles out of his jacket, hides in a watering can, and finally squeezes under the gate.

questions.q: How does Peter feel during the chase? Give evidence.
questions.a: Frightened — he cries big tears in the net, and he is trembling and lost in the garden.

days.guide: Teach irregular past tense from the story (ran, went, ate, hid, sat, told, found) and complete 10 sentences. Sort oi/oy words.

questions.q: Past tense of hide and eat?
questions.a: hid; ate.

questions.q: Fix: 'Peter runned under the gate.'
questions.a: Peter ran under the gate.

days.guide: Discuss the ending: Peter is sick and gets camomile tea while his sisters get bread, milk, and blackberries. Ask what lesson it teaches. The child rewrites the ending as if Peter had listened.

questions.q: How does the ending show Peter's consequence?
questions.a: He loses his jacket and shoes, feels sick, and is put to bed with camomile tea while Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cotton-tail have bread, milk, and blackberries.

questions.q: What lesson does the story teach?
questions.a: Listen to your parents' warnings; disobeying can bring trouble.

days.guide: Give the spelling check and past-tense quiz. Read The Tale of Benjamin Bunny aloud and the child fills a story map.

questions.q: Why do Benjamin and Peter go into the garden?
questions.a: To get Peter's clothes back from the scarecrow.

questions.q: Who rescues them from the cat?
questions.a: Old Mr. Benjamin Bunny, Benjamin's father.

weeks.assessment_key: Story map for The Tale of Benjamin Bunny: Characters — Benjamin Bunny, Peter Rabbit, the cat, old Mr. Benjamin Bunny; Setting — Mr. McGregor's garden; Problem — Peter wants his clothes back from the scarecrow and the boys get trapped under a basket by a cat; Ending — Benjamin's father rescues them and takes them home. Irregular past tense (10): run/ran, go/went, eat/ate, hide/hid, sit/sat, tell/told, find/found, see/saw, come/came, get/got. Spelling: coin, boil, soil, point, join, boy, toy, joy, enjoy, oyster (8+ proficient).

weeks.prep: Get The Velveteen Rabbit (Margery Williams, public domain) and read it first; note that the Boy's illness (scarlet fever) and the burning of his toys may be sad for some children. Make a character-change chart and oo/au/aw word cards (moon, food, book, look, sauce, haul, draw, paw). Print a story-mountain organizer.
misconceptions: Thinking 'Real' in the story means 'alive' from the start. Reread the Skin Horse: becoming Real happens when a child loves you for a long, long time.
Reading oo with only one sound. Sort moon/food (long oo) vs. book/look (short oo).

days.guide: Read the first half aloud. Discuss what the Skin Horse means by 'Real.' Read oo words both ways.

questions.q: According to the Skin Horse, how does a toy become Real?
questions.a: When a child loves it for a long, long time — not just to play with, but really loves it.

questions.q: Does becoming Real hurt, according to the Skin Horse?
questions.a: Sometimes, but when you are Real you don't mind being hurt.

days.guide: Finish the story and chart how the Rabbit changes (new and shiny → shabby and loved → a real rabbit). Read au/aw words.

questions.q: How does the Rabbit change by the end?
questions.a: He goes from a new toy, to a worn toy the Boy loves, to a real living rabbit made Real by the Fairy.

questions.q: Why were the Boy's toys taken away?
questions.a: The Boy had scarlet fever, and the doctor ordered his toys burned so the germs would not spread.

days.guide: Write 5 sentences retelling the Rabbit's adventures with irregular past verbs (was, became, went, grew, saw). Read them aloud to check.

questions.q: Fix: 'The Rabbit becomed Real.'
questions.a: The Rabbit became Real.

questions.q: Past tense of grow and see?
questions.a: grew; saw.

days.guide: Plan an original story about a toy or animal on a story mountain: beginning, problem, events, solution, ending.

questions.q: What goes at the top of the story mountain?
questions.a: The most exciting part — the biggest moment of the problem.

questions.q: Give a sample problem for a toy story.
questions.a: Example: A stuffed bear gets left behind at the park.

days.guide: The child answers who/what/why questions in writing, takes the spelling check, and shares the story plan.

questions.q: Who helped the Rabbit become a real rabbit?
questions.a: The nursery magic Fairy.

questions.q: Spell 'book' and 'draw.'
questions.a: b-o-o-k; d-r-a-w.

weeks.assessment_key: Written answers (model): Who gave the Boy the rabbit? It was in his Christmas stocking. What does Real mean to the Skin Horse? When a child loves you for a long, long time, you become Real. Why was the Rabbit thrown out? The Boy had scarlet fever, and the doctor said his toys had to be burned. How did the Rabbit become a real rabbit? The nursery magic Fairy came when he cried a real tear and made him Real. Spelling (suggested 12): moon, food, soon, book, look, foot, sauce, haul, draw, paw, saw, lawn. Story plan: proficient has character, setting, problem, 2–3 events, and solution.

weeks.prep: Get Chrysanthemum (Kevin Henkes) and preview it. Collect paint-chip strips from a hardware store for word ladders, and soft c/g word cards (city, cent, face, rice, gem, giant, page, cage).
misconceptions: Mixing up adjectives and adverbs. Ask: 'Does it tell about a thing (adjective) or about how someone does something (adverb)?' Many adverbs end in -ly.
Using 'very' for every strong feeling. Use shades of meaning: glad → happy → thrilled.

days.guide: Read Chrysanthemum. Using the pictures, the child shows how her feelings change from home to school each day. Discuss why words can hurt or help.

questions.q: Why does Chrysanthemum stop loving her name?
questions.a: The kids at school tease her because her name is long (13 letters) and she is named after a flower.

questions.q: What makes her love her name again?
questions.a: Mrs. Twinkle, the music teacher, says her own name is long and she is named after a flower too, and she might name her baby Chrysanthemum.

days.guide: Order feeling words on paint chips (glad, happy, thrilled; sad, upset, miserable) and verbs (toss, throw, hurl). Use 3 in sentences about Chrysanthemum.

questions.q: Order from weakest to strongest: thrilled, glad, happy.
questions.a: glad, happy, thrilled.

questions.q: Use a strong feeling word in a sentence about Chrysanthemum.
questions.a: Example: Chrysanthemum felt miserable when the kids laughed at her name.

days.guide: Teach adjectives (describe nouns) and adverbs (describe verbs). Sort 12 words and write 4 sentences. Read soft c and g words.

questions.q: In 'She walked slowly,' is slowly an adjective or adverb?
questions.a: Adverb — it tells how she walked.

questions.q: In 'a long name,' what kind of word is long?
questions.a: An adjective — it describes the noun name.

days.guide: Draft the fiction story from the plan with 3 adjectives, 2 adverbs, and dialogue. The beginning introduces character and setting.

questions.q: Write a beginning sentence that introduces character and setting.
questions.a: Example: Bear lived on a shelf in Mia's sunny bedroom.

questions.q: Add an adverb: 'The dog barked.'
questions.a: Example: The dog barked loudly.

days.guide: Give the spelling check and adjective/adverb quiz. The child rereads the draft aloud and adds one feeling word.

questions.q: Adjective or adverb: quickly, purple?
questions.a: quickly — adverb; purple — adjective.

questions.q: Spell 'city' and 'page.'
questions.a: c-i-t-y; p-a-g-e.

weeks.assessment_key: Adjective/adverb quiz (suggested 12): adjectives — long, tiny, purple, happy, loud, soft; adverbs — slowly, quickly, loudly, gently, happily, quietly. Spelling (suggested): city, cent, face, rice, ice, gem, giant, page, cage, huge. Draft check: beginning introduces character and setting; at least 3 adjectives, 2 adverbs, and some dialogue.

weeks.prep: Get Ira Sleeps Over (Bernard Waber). Make a revision checklist (capitals, end marks, quotation marks, past-tense verbs, unit spelling patterns), construction paper and a stapler. Choose an on-level passage (about 100 words) for the fluency check and a short new story with questions for the unit test.
misconceptions: Giving vague feedback ('It's good'). Teach 'star and wish': one specific good thing and one specific thing to improve.
Placing quotation marks around the speaker tag ('"said Mom"'). Only the spoken words go inside.

days.guide: Read Ira Sleeps Over. Discuss how Ira responds to his sister's teasing and how he decides about his teddy bear. Practice irregular words (could, would, should, through, though).

questions.q: Why does Ira decide not to take his teddy bear at first?
questions.a: His sister says Reggie will laugh at him and think he's a baby.

questions.q: What changes Ira's mind?
questions.a: Reggie gets out his own teddy bear (Foo Foo) at bedtime, so Ira goes home to get his bear, Tah Tah.

days.guide: The child reads the story draft to a family member who gives one star and one wish. Revise based on the wish.

questions.q: Give an example of a helpful 'wish.'
questions.a: Example: 'I wish you told how the bear felt when it was lost.'

questions.q: What do you do with a wish?
questions.a: Use it to revise — add or change that part.

days.guide: Edit with the checklist: capitals, end marks, quotation marks, unit spelling patterns, past-tense verbs.

questions.q: Punctuate: Where is my bear asked Ira
questions.a: "Where is my bear?" asked Ira.

questions.q: Fix: 'He goed home.'
questions.a: He went home.

days.guide: Publish the story as a stapled book with cover, title page, and illustrations. Practice reading it aloud 3 times.

questions.q: What goes on a title page?
questions.a: The title and the author's (and illustrator's) name.

questions.q: Why practice reading aloud 3 times?
questions.a: To read smoothly with expression.

days.guide: Give the one-minute fluency check and the unit test on a new story.

questions.q: How do you count words correct per minute?
questions.a: Count the words read in one minute and subtract the errors.

questions.q: How did Ira feel at the end of Ira Sleeps Over?
questions.a: Happy and comfortable — he and Reggie both had their bears and fell asleep.

weeks.assessment_key: Fluency: count words correct per minute on the passage (goal about 70–90 WCPM mid-grade 2); note expression (1–3). Narrative rubric (3 = proficient): beginning introduces character/setting; problem and events in order; solution and ending; descriptive words and dialogue; mostly correct conventions. Unit test: character response explained with text evidence; beginning/ending described; adjectives and adverbs correctly identified.

weeks.prep: Get A Child's Garden of Verses (Robert Louis Stevenson, public domain) and mark 'My Shadow,' 'The Swing,' 'Rain,' and 'Where Go the Boats?' Have a drum or pot to tap the beat. Make a list of 10 compound words. Pick a new short rhyming poem for Friday.
misconceptions: Thinking any two words that end with the same letter rhyme (cow/snow). Say them aloud — rhymes share the same ending sound.
Splitting compound words at the wrong spot (no-tebook). Look for two real words: note + book.

days.guide: Read 'My Shadow' aloud and tap the beat. Highlight rhyming pairs at the line ends. Discuss what the shadow does.

questions.q: Name a rhyming pair from the first stanza of 'My Shadow.'
questions.a: me/see or head/bed.

questions.q: What does the shadow do that is funny?
questions.a: It grows taller or smaller — sometimes it shoots up tall like a rubber ball and sometimes there's none of it at all.

days.guide: Read 'The Swing' while swinging arms to the beat. Discuss how the beat feels like swinging. Split and define compound words.

questions.q: How does the rhythm of 'The Swing' feel like swinging?
questions.a: The beat goes up and down, back and forth, like a swing.

questions.q: Split 'playground.'
questions.a: play + ground — ground where you play.

days.guide: Use smaller words to define 10 compound words. Write a rhyming couplet with one.

questions.q: What does 'bookshelf' mean?
questions.a: A shelf that holds books.

questions.q: Write a rhyming couplet using 'rainbow.'
questions.a: Example: I saw a rainbow in the sky, / its colors bright and way up high.

days.guide: Memorize the first stanza of 'My Shadow' and practice reciting with expression and volume. Read 'Rain' and 'Where Go the Boats?' for fun.

questions.q: What does reciting with expression mean?
questions.a: Saying it with feeling, changing your voice to match the words.

questions.q: In 'Where Go the Boats?', what does the child float on the river?
questions.a: Boats (toy boats) that float away down the river.

days.guide: The child recites the stanza, finds rhymes and beats in a new poem, and takes the spelling check.

questions.q: How do you know two words rhyme?
questions.a: They have the same ending sound (bed/head).

questions.q: Spell 'notebook' and 'sunshine.'
questions.a: n-o-t-e-b-o-o-k; s-u-n-s-h-i-n-e.

weeks.assessment_key: Recitation rubric (3 = proficient): first stanza of 'My Shadow' recited with no more than 1–2 prompts, with expression, and loud enough to hear. New poem: child names rhyming pairs at line ends and taps a steady beat. Spelling (suggested 10): sunshine, rainbow, playground, birdhouse, bookshelf, notebook, cupcake, bedroom, backpack, football.

weeks.prep: Get Where the Sidewalk Ends (Shel Silverstein) or a library poetry anthology, Mother Goose rhymes, and the 'Peter Piper' tongue twister. Copy Christina Rossetti's 'Who Has Seen the Wind?' Prepare a mid-year phonics inventory (vowel teams, r-controlled, two-syllable words) and a fluency passage.
misconceptions: Thinking alliteration means words that rhyme. Alliteration repeats the BEGINNING sound (Peter Piper picked).
Splitting two-syllable words between vowel-team letters (ra-in-coat). Keep vowel teams together: rain-coat.

days.guide: Read 'Peter Piper' and Mother Goose rhymes. Underline repeated beginning sounds. The child writes an alliterative sentence about their name.

questions.q: What sound repeats in 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers'?
questions.a: The /p/ sound.

questions.q: Write an alliterative sentence for the name Sam.
questions.a: Example: Silly Sam sings sweet songs.

days.guide: Read Rossetti's 'Who Has Seen the Wind?' Discuss how the repeated question gives rhythm and meaning.

questions.q: How do we know the wind is there if no one sees it?
questions.a: The leaves hang trembling and the trees bow down their heads — we see what the wind does.

questions.q: Why does the poet repeat 'Who has seen the wind?'
questions.a: It makes a rhythm and reminds us that no one can see the wind itself.

days.guide: Split two-syllable words (re-peat, pa-per, rain-coat, ex-plain) and read 20. Clap syllables in poem lines.

questions.q: Split 'paper' and 'raincoat.'
questions.a: pa-per; rain-coat.

questions.q: How many syllables in 'explain'?
questions.a: 2 (ex-plain).

days.guide: Write a list poem 'Things I Hear at Night' with describing words and a repeated line. Illustrate it.

questions.q: Give a line for a night-sounds list poem.
questions.a: Example: the tick-tock of the hallway clock.

questions.q: What is a repeated line?
questions.a: A line used more than once, like 'At night I hear…'

days.guide: Give the mid-year phonics inventory, a fluency read, and the poem comprehension question.

questions.q: What does repetition do in a poem?
questions.a: It gives rhythm and makes an idea stand out.

questions.q: Read and split 'repeat.'
questions.a: re-peat.

weeks.assessment_key: Mid-year phonics inventory: record correct/incorrect for vowel teams (rain, play, tree, beach, boat, snow), r-controlled (car, corn, her, bird, turn), and two-syllable words (repeat, paper, raincoat, explain); note patterns to review. Fluency: record WCPM and compare to fall. Poem question: 'Why does Rossetti repeat "Who has seen the wind?"' — model answer: the repeated question gives the poem a rhythm and reminds us we can't see the wind, only what it does (leaves trembling, trees bowing). List poem rubric: 3 = 6+ items about night sounds with describing words and a repeated line.

weeks.prep: Mark Stevenson's 'Rain' and 'Windy Nights' in A Child's Garden of Verses. Make a five-senses chart and gather a rainstick or bell. Write 8 sentence pairs to combine and a list of -ed/-ing words (jumped, played, wanted, running, hopping, sitting).
misconceptions: Joining sentences with 'and' but no comma, or using 'and' for everything. Show that 'but' shows a difference and 'so' shows a result.
Thinking -ed always sounds like /ed/. Sort jumped (/t/), played (/d/), and wanted (/ed/).

days.guide: Go outside and list what you see, hear, smell, feel, and taste. Turn the list into a 5-line senses poem. Read 'Rain' and 'Windy Nights' as models.

questions.q: In Stevenson's 'Rain,' where does the rain fall?
questions.a: All around — on field and tree, on the umbrellas here, and on the ships at sea.

questions.q: Write a 'hear' line for a senses poem.
questions.a: Example: I hear the birds chirping in the oak tree.

days.guide: Teach joining two sentences with a comma and and, but, or, so. Combine 8 pairs. Practice doubling before -ing (run → running).

questions.q: Combine: 'I was hungry. I ate an apple.'
questions.a: I was hungry, so I ate an apple.

questions.q: Add -ing to 'hop.'
questions.a: hopping (double the p).

days.guide: Read -ed words and sort by sound: /t/ jumped, /d/ played, /ed/ wanted. Use 3 in compound sentences.

questions.q: What sound does -ed make in 'wanted'?
questions.a: /ed/ (an extra syllable).

questions.q: Sort: jumped, played.
questions.a: jumped — /t/; played — /d/.

days.guide: Revise the senses poem by swapping 3 plain words for stronger words (said → whispered, big → enormous). Read both versions aloud.

questions.q: Give a stronger word for 'big.'
questions.a: enormous, huge, or gigantic.

questions.q: Give a stronger word for 'went.'
questions.a: Examples: raced, wandered, tiptoed.

days.guide: Give the -ed/-ing spelling check and compound-sentence quiz. The child reads the revised poem aloud.

questions.q: Combine: 'I like dogs. My sister likes cats.'
questions.a: I like dogs, but my sister likes cats.

questions.q: Spell 'running' and 'played.'
questions.a: r-u-n-n-i-n-g; p-l-a-y-e-d.

weeks.assessment_key: Compound-sentence quiz (suggested): 1) The wind blew. The leaves fell. → The wind blew, and the leaves fell. 2) I wanted to play. It was raining. → I wanted to play, but it was raining. 3) We can read. We can draw. → We can read, or we can draw. 4) I was tired. I went to bed. → I was tired, so I went to bed. Spelling (suggested 12): jumped, played, wanted, looked, rained, landed, running, hopping, sitting, swimming, getting, stopping. Revised poem: 3 plain words replaced with stronger words.

weeks.prep: Gather a phone or tablet for audio recording, a folder for the anthology, and drawing supplies. Make compound/two-syllable word bingo cards. Choose a new short poem with rhyme, alliteration, and repetition for the unit test.
misconceptions: Reading poems too fast. Mark slashes for pauses and practice breathing at line ends.
Copying poems without the poet's name. Every poem in the anthology needs its title and author.

days.guide: Choose 5 favorite poems from the unit (your own and published) and copy them neatly with title and author.

questions.q: What two things must be with each poem?
questions.a: The title and the poet's name.

questions.q: Who wrote 'My Shadow'?
questions.a: Robert Louis Stevenson.

days.guide: Practice reading each poem at the right pace with expression; mark pauses with slashes. Play compound/two-syllable bingo.

questions.q: What does a slash mark in a poem show you?
questions.a: Where to pause.

questions.q: Split 'rainbow.'
questions.a: rain-bow.

days.guide: Record 3 poems, listen back to self-assess pace and volume, and re-record one to improve it.

questions.q: What should you listen for in your recording?
questions.a: Pace (not too fast), volume (loud enough), and expression.

questions.q: If you rushed, what should you do?
questions.a: Slow down and pause at the slashes and line ends.

days.guide: Add illustrations and a table of contents. Write one sentence for each poem explaining why you chose it.

questions.q: What goes in a table of contents?
questions.a: Poem titles and their page numbers, in order.

questions.q: Write a 'why I chose it' sentence.
questions.a: Example: I chose 'The Swing' because it reminds me of the park.

days.guide: Hold a poetry café: the child performs 2 poems. Give the unit test on a new poem and the 15-word spelling test.

questions.q: What is alliteration?
questions.a: Repeating the same beginning sound in nearby words.

questions.q: What is repetition in a poem?
questions.a: Using the same word or line more than once.

weeks.assessment_key: Anthology and recording rubric (3 = proficient): 5 poems copied neatly with titles and authors, table of contents, illustrations, a 'why I chose it' sentence for each; recording read at a good pace, clear volume, with expression. Unit test on the new poem: correctly identify one rhyming pair, one example of alliteration, and one repeated line or word. Spelling (suggested 15): sunshine, rainbow, notebook, playground, raincoat, paper, repeat, explain, jumped, played, wanted, running, hopping, sitting, swimming.

weeks.prep: Get Perrault's Cinderella (Andrew Lang's The Blue Fairy Book, public domain) and Yeh-Shen (Ai-Ling Louie); read both first. Draw a large Venn diagram and make prefix cards (un-, re-, dis-).
misconceptions: Thinking every Cinderella story has a fairy godmother. Point out different magic helpers: a fairy godmother in Perrault, magic fish bones in Yeh-Shen.
Thinking a prefix can go on any word. Check that the new word makes sense (unhappy, but not 'unrun').

days.guide: Read Perrault's Cinderella and list the story parts: kind girl, mean family, magic helper, event, lost item, happy ending. Teach un- (not).

questions.q: Who helps Cinderella go to the ball?
questions.a: Her fairy godmother, who turns a pumpkin into a coach and mice into horses.

questions.q: What must Cinderella remember at the ball?
questions.a: To leave before midnight, when the magic ends.

days.guide: Read Yeh-Shen and use illustrations to describe the setting (long ago in China). Teach re- (again).

questions.q: What is Yeh-Shen's magic helper?
questions.a: The bones of her fish friend, which grant wishes.

questions.q: What does re- mean in 'retell'?
questions.a: Again — retell means tell again.

days.guide: Fill the Venn diagram comparing Cinderella and Yeh-Shen. Teach dis- (not/opposite).

questions.q: Name one way the two stories are alike.
questions.a: Both girls are mistreated by a stepmother, lose a slipper at a big event, and are found by it.

questions.q: Name one difference.
questions.a: Cinderella's helper is a fairy godmother; Yeh-Shen's is magic fish bones (or glass slipper vs. golden slippers).

days.guide: Use prefixes to define 12 words and use 4 in sentences. Partner talk: which magic helper is more interesting and why?

questions.q: What does 'disagree' mean?
questions.a: To not agree.

questions.q: What does 'unlock' mean?
questions.a: To open a lock (the opposite of lock).

days.guide: The child writes 1 way the stories are alike and 2 ways they differ, then takes the prefix spelling check.

questions.q: Write a contrast sentence.
questions.a: Example: Cinderella wore glass slippers, but Yeh-Shen wore golden slippers.

questions.q: Spell 'unhappy' and 'reread.'
questions.a: u-n-h-a-p-p-y; r-e-r-e-a-d.

weeks.assessment_key: Venn diagram (model): Cinderella only — France, fairy godmother, pumpkin coach, glass slipper, must leave by midnight, a ball at the palace. Yeh-Shen only — China, magic fish bones, golden slippers, a festival, a king finds her. Both — kind girl treated badly by a stepmother/stepfamily, a magic helper, a big event she goes to in secret, she loses a slipper, the slipper helps find her, happy ending. Written sentences: 1 alike, 2 different. Spelling (suggested 12): unhappy, unlock, undo, unkind, reread, retell, rebuild, redo, dislike, disagree, disappear, unfair.

weeks.prep: Get Mufaro's Beautiful Daughters (John Steptoe), The Rough-Face Girl (Rafe Martin), and Adelita (Tomie dePaola); read each first. Make a comparison chart (title, place, main character, helper, test, ending) for 5 versions. Suffix cards: -ful, -less, -ly, -er.
misconceptions: Opinions with no reasons ('I like it because I like it'). Reasons must come from the book: 'because Nyasha is kind to everyone she meets.'
Talking over others in discussion. Practice: wait, listen, then add on ('I agree, and…').

days.guide: Read Mufaro's Beautiful Daughters and add it to the chart. Teach -ful (full of) and -less (without).

questions.q: How are Nyasha and Manyara different?
questions.a: Nyasha is kind and generous; Manyara is selfish and rude.

questions.q: How does the king test the sisters?
questions.a: He appears in disguise (a hungry boy, an old woman, and the snake Nyoka) to see who is kind; Nyasha is kind, so she becomes queen.

days.guide: Read The Rough-Face Girl and add it to the chart. Discuss what 'seeing' the Invisible Being means. Teach -ly.

questions.q: Why is the girl called Rough-Face?
questions.a: Her face and hands were scarred by sparks from the fire her sisters made her tend.

questions.q: What does 'seeing' the Invisible Being mean?
questions.a: Seeing his greatness in nature with a true heart — she sees his bow is the rainbow and his sled runner is the Milky Way.

days.guide: Read Adelita and add it to the chart. Teach -er meaning 'one who.'

questions.q: Who helps Adelita?
questions.a: Esperanza, the kind woman who cared for her since she was a baby.

questions.q: What does 'farmer' mean?
questions.a: One who farms.

days.guide: Discuss your favorite Cinderella story, giving reasons from the text and taking turns. Write the opinion sentence and 2 reasons.

questions.q: Write an opinion sentence with a reason.
questions.a: Example: My favorite is Mufaro's Beautiful Daughters because Nyasha's kindness wins in the end.

questions.q: How do you build on someone's idea?
questions.a: Say 'I agree, and…' or 'I see it differently because…'

days.guide: Complete the chart for 5 versions and write which two are most alike. Give the suffix spelling check.

questions.q: Which two versions both use a lost slipper?
questions.a: Cinderella and Yeh-Shen.

questions.q: Spell 'helpful' and 'quickly.'
questions.a: h-e-l-p-f-u-l; q-u-i-c-k-l-y.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison chart (model): Mufaro's Beautiful Daughters — Zimbabwe; Nyasha; helper/test: the king tests the sisters in disguise (hungry boy, old woman, snake Nyoka); kind Nyasha becomes queen. The Rough-Face Girl — Algonquin; the Rough-Face Girl; test: tell what the Invisible Being's bow and sled runner are made of; she sees him in nature (the rainbow and the Milky Way) and marries him. Adelita — Mexico; Adelita; helper: Esperanza, her loving old nanny; event: a fiesta; she marries Javier. Plus Cinderella (France) and Yeh-Shen (China) from last week. Opinion: proficient states a favorite and 2 reasons from the text. Spelling (suggested 12): helpful, careful, hopeful, careless, helpless, kindly, quickly, slowly, teacher, farmer, painter, singer.

weeks.prep: Get The Three Little Pigs (traditional) and The True Story of the 3 Little Pigs! (Jon Scieszka). Have Cinderella and the opinion organizer handy. Pick a short new fable for Friday (e.g., 'The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse').
misconceptions: Thinking point of view only means 'I' or 'he.' Ask 'Who is telling this story, and what do they think happened?'
Opinion drafts with reasons but no linking words. Add because, also, another reason, and finally.

days.guide: Read The Three Little Pigs and retell it from the pigs' point of view, practicing voices for each pig and the wolf.

questions.q: Why does the third pig's house stand?
questions.a: It is made of bricks, which the wolf can't blow down.

questions.q: How would the pigs describe the wolf?
questions.a: Big, bad, and mean — he tries to blow their houses down and eat them.

days.guide: Read The True Story of the 3 Little Pigs!. Chart what the pigs think vs. what the wolf claims.

questions.q: Why does the wolf say he went to the pigs' houses?
questions.a: To borrow a cup of sugar for his granny's birthday cake.

questions.q: What does the wolf blame for blowing the houses down?
questions.a: A bad cold that made him sneeze.

days.guide: Retell a Cinderella scene in 4–5 sentences from a stepsister's point of view and read it in her voice.

questions.q: Write a first sentence from a stepsister's view.
questions.a: Example: I could not believe the prince only danced with that mysterious girl!

questions.q: What word should a first-person retelling use?
questions.a: I (me, my).

days.guide: Draft 'The Best Cinderella Story' with an opening, opinion, 3 reasons with linking words, and a conclusion.

questions.q: Name 3 linking words for reasons.
questions.a: because, also, another reason (or finally).

questions.q: What does the concluding sentence do?
questions.a: Restates the opinion.

days.guide: Read a new fable and tell how two characters see the event differently. Check the opinion draft for linking words.

questions.q: In 'The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse,' how does each mouse see city life?
questions.a: The town mouse loves its rich food; the country mouse thinks it is too scary and dangerous.

questions.q: Find the linking words in: 'I like it because it is funny. Also, the pictures are bright.'
questions.a: because, also.

weeks.assessment_key: Point-of-view retelling (stepsister): proficient = 4–5 sentences in first person ('I') that show the stepsister's feelings and stay true to story events. Opinion draft: opening, clear opinion, 3 reasons with at least 3 linking words (because, also, another reason), and a conclusion. New fable check (Town Mouse and Country Mouse): the town mouse thinks the country is boring and plain; the country mouse thinks the city is too dangerous — she prefers a simple, safe life.

weeks.prep: Have opinion drafts, poster paper, markers, and the Cinderella books. Prepare a unit test: two short versions of a folktale, 15 prefix/suffix words to read, and point-of-view questions.
misconceptions: Writing 'more taller' or 'happyest.' Teach -er for 2 things, -est for 3 or more, and change y to i (happier, happiest).
Reasons without book evidence. Ask 'Which page shows that?'

days.guide: Teach -er and -est (tall, taller, tallest; happy, happier, happiest). Compare Cinderella characters with comparatives.

questions.q: Complete: tall, ___, ___.
questions.a: taller, tallest.

questions.q: Complete: happy, ___, ___.
questions.a: happier, happiest (change y to i).

days.guide: Strengthen reasons with book examples and add a closing that restates the opinion. Check each reason starts with a linking word.

questions.q: Strengthen: 'Yeh-Shen is good because it's nice.'
questions.a: Example: Yeh-Shen is the best because her fish friend's magic bones help her, which shows kindness is rewarded.

questions.q: What does a strong closing do?
questions.a: Restates the opinion in new words.

days.guide: Edit for capitals, end marks, and prefix/suffix spelling. Publish as a poster with a book-cover drawing.

questions.q: Fix: 'i think yeh-shen is the best'
questions.a: I think Yeh-Shen is the best.

questions.q: Spell 'careful.'
questions.a: c-a-r-e-f-u-l.

days.guide: Present the poster to family and answer one question; listen to a family member's opinion and ask about their reasons.

questions.q: Give a question about someone's reasons.
questions.a: Example: 'Why do you think that part was the most exciting?'

questions.q: What should a listener do?
questions.a: Look at the speaker, listen without interrupting, then ask a question.

days.guide: Give the unit test: compare two folktale versions, decode 15 words, identify point of view.

questions.q: Who tells The True Story of the 3 Little Pigs!?
questions.a: The wolf (Alexander T. Wolf).

questions.q: What does the suffix -less mean?
questions.a: Without.

weeks.assessment_key: Opinion poster rubric (3 = proficient): opinion clearly stated; 3 reasons each with an example from a book; linking words; closing restates opinion; mostly correct capitals, end marks, prefix/suffix spelling. Unit test: comparison chart correctly completed for the two versions with 2 sentences; 13/15 prefix/suffix words decoded; point of view identified (who is telling the story).

weeks.prep: Get A Picture Book of Martin Luther King, Jr. (David A. Adler) and read it first. Parent preview: it explains segregation and that Dr. King was shot and killed in 1968 — be ready to talk about it calmly. Make a timeline strip, reflexive-pronoun sentences, and -le word cards. Print a ReadWorks biography passage.
misconceptions: Thinking a biography is made up. A biography is a true story of a real person's life, told in order.
Using 'hisself' or 'theirselves.' Correct forms: himself, themselves.

days.guide: Read the book and learn that a biography tells a real person's life in order. List 5 important events.

questions.q: Where and when was Martin Luther King Jr. born?
questions.a: In Atlanta, Georgia, in 1929.

questions.q: What unfair laws did Dr. King work against?
questions.a: Segregation laws that kept Black and white people apart and treated Black people unfairly.

days.guide: Put events on a timeline strip and explain how one led to the next.

questions.q: What happened after Rosa Parks was arrested?
questions.a: Dr. King helped lead the Montgomery bus boycott; people stopped riding the buses until the law changed.

questions.q: What famous speech did Dr. King give at the March on Washington?
questions.a: The 'I Have a Dream' speech (1963).

days.guide: Teach reflexive pronouns and complete 10 sentences. Read -le words.

questions.q: Complete: She made the card by ___.
questions.a: herself.

questions.q: Complete: We cleaned the room ___.
questions.a: ourselves.

days.guide: Reread 2 pages; the child writes what each paragraph is mostly about. Discuss why Dr. King believed in peaceful protest.

questions.q: Why did Dr. King believe in peaceful protest?
questions.a: He believed nonviolence and love could change unfair laws without hurting people.

questions.q: How do you find what a paragraph is mostly about?
questions.a: Ask what most of the sentences tell about.

days.guide: The child answers 5 who/what/when/why/how questions on a biography passage, takes the -le spelling check, and the reflexive quiz.

questions.q: Fix: 'He did it hisself.'
questions.a: He did it himself.

questions.q: Spell 'little' and 'purple.'
questions.a: l-i-t-t-l-e; p-u-r-p-l-e.

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline (model order): 1929 born in Atlanta, Georgia → grew up facing unfair segregation laws → became a minister → 1955–56 led the Montgomery bus boycott after Rosa Parks's arrest → 1963 March on Washington, 'I Have a Dream' speech → 1964 Nobel Peace Prize → 1968 killed in Memphis. Cause/effect: unfair laws → boycott → laws changed. Reflexive pronouns (10): I → myself, you → yourself, he → himself, she → herself, we → ourselves, they → themselves. Spelling (suggested 10): table, little, simple, apple, purple, candle, bubble, puzzle, turtle, middle.

weeks.prep: Get I Am Rosa Parks and I Am Jackie Robinson (Brad Meltzer). Make a contractions chart and a research folder. Plan a library trip to find 2 sources on a chosen person.
misconceptions: Putting the apostrophe where letters were not removed (did'nt). The apostrophe replaces the missing letter: didn't (did not).
Research questions that can be answered yes/no. Start with when, where, what, how, why.

days.guide: Read I Am Rosa Parks and discuss why her choice on the bus mattered. Answer how/why questions in complete sentences.

questions.q: What did Rosa Parks refuse to do in 1955?
questions.a: Give up her bus seat to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama.

questions.q: Why did her choice matter?
questions.a: It sparked the Montgomery bus boycott, which helped end segregation on buses.

days.guide: Read I Am Jackie Robinson and compare his courage with Rosa's. Teach contractions.

questions.q: What barrier did Jackie Robinson break in 1947?
questions.a: He became the first Black player in modern Major League Baseball (with the Brooklyn Dodgers).

questions.q: How was Jackie's courage like Rosa's?
questions.a: Both faced unfair treatment calmly and bravely without fighting back, and helped change things.

days.guide: Choose a person to research (e.g., Cesar Chavez, Sally Ride, Abraham Lincoln, Helen Keller, Marie Curie) and find 2 sources.

questions.q: Why use 2 sources?
questions.a: To find more facts and check that facts agree.

questions.q: What did Sally Ride do?
questions.a: She was the first American woman to fly in space (1983).

days.guide: Write 3 research questions and start notes from the first source.

questions.q: Write a research question about Helen Keller.
questions.a: Example: How did Helen Keller learn to communicate?

questions.q: Turn into a note: 'Abraham Lincoln was born in a log cabin in Kentucky in 1809.'
questions.a: born 1809, log cabin, Kentucky.

days.guide: Give the contractions quiz, a read-aloud fluency check, and a research-notes check.

questions.q: What two words make 'they're'?
questions.a: they are.

questions.q: Write the contraction for 'did not.'
questions.a: didn't.

weeks.assessment_key: Contractions quiz (12): can't (cannot), didn't (did not), he's (he is), they're (they are), I'm (I am), we'll (we will), isn't (is not), don't (do not), it's (it is), you're (you are), wasn't (was not), she'll (she will). Fluency: record WCPM on a biography page. Research sheet: 3 open questions written; notes are key words with the source title.

weeks.prep: Get Harvesting Hope: The Story of Cesar Chavez (Kathleen Krull) and read it first. Gather index cards in 4 colors (early life, challenge, actions, legacy) and a second source on the child's research person.
misconceptions: Using 's for plurals (two dog's). 's shows ownership: the dog's bone.
Not capitalizing holidays and places. Names of specific days, cities, and states get capitals: Labor Day, Delano, California.

days.guide: Read Harvesting Hope. Notice the order of events and why Chavez's march mattered. Identify the author's purpose.

questions.q: Why did Cesar Chavez lead a march?
questions.a: To get fair pay and better treatment for farmworkers.

questions.q: Where did the march go?
questions.a: From Delano to Sacramento, California's capital — about 340 miles.

days.guide: Take notes from a second source and add new facts to note cards (early life, challenge, actions, legacy).

questions.q: What is a legacy?
questions.a: What a person is remembered for and the difference they left behind.

questions.q: What was Cesar Chavez's childhood like?
questions.a: His family lost their farm in Arizona and became migrant farmworkers in California.

days.guide: Teach singular possessives ('s) and capitals for holidays, places, and names. Fix 10 sentences.

questions.q: Fix: 'cesars march went to sacramento.'
questions.a: Cesar's march went to Sacramento.

questions.q: Write the possessive: the bus that belongs to Rosa.
questions.a: Rosa's bus.

days.guide: Sort note cards into 3 groups (early life, big work, why we remember them) and plan a paragraph for each.

questions.q: Which group: 'born in 1927'?
questions.a: Early life.

questions.q: Which group: 'led a march for farmworkers'?
questions.a: Big work.

days.guide: Draft the first paragraph of the biography report and take the spelling check.

questions.q: What should paragraph 1 start with?
questions.a: A topic sentence introducing the person and early life.

questions.q: Spell 'California.'
questions.a: C-a-l-i-f-o-r-n-i-a.

weeks.assessment_key: Note cards sorted into 3 groups with at least 3 facts each. First paragraph rubric: 3 = topic sentence about early life + 3 facts in own words; 2 = facts without topic sentence; 1 = copied or off topic. Capitalization/possessive check (suggested): Rosa's bus, Cesar's march, Jackie's team, Labor Day, Delano, California, Fourth of July, Atlanta, Georgia, the girl's book. Spelling: can't, don't, it's, I'm, Sacramento, Mexico, Arizona (8+ of 12 proficient).

weeks.prep: Gather poster board, markers, the child's notes, and simple dress-up items for a 'living museum.' Prepare a new short biography passage with questions for Friday.
misconceptions: Speeches read too fast or too quietly. Practice with a timer and 'speak to the back of the room.'
Timelines out of order. Number events first, then copy them onto the poster.

days.guide: Write the 'big work' and 'why we remember them' paragraphs with facts and a concluding sentence.

questions.q: Write a concluding sentence about Cesar Chavez.
questions.a: Example: Cesar Chavez is remembered for helping farmworkers get fair treatment.

questions.q: What does the 'why we remember them' paragraph tell?
questions.a: How the person changed things and why they still matter.

days.guide: Revise for order and clarity; edit for capitals, apostrophes, and spelling. Make a final copy.

questions.q: Fix: 'sally ride flew in space in 1983'
questions.a: Sally Ride flew in space in 1983.

questions.q: Why check the order of sentences?
questions.a: So the life story makes sense from beginning to end.

days.guide: Make a poster with a portrait, a 5-event timeline, and a quote or fact box.

questions.q: How should timeline events be arranged?
