questions.a: In order from earliest to latest.

questions.q: What goes in a fact box?
questions.a: An interesting fact or a quote by the person.

days.guide: Rehearse a 1-minute first-person speech ('I am Sally Ride…'), speaking audibly in complete sentences.

questions.q: Start a living museum speech as Abraham Lincoln.
questions.a: Example: I am Abraham Lincoln. I was the 16th President of the United States.

questions.q: Why speak in first person?
questions.a: Because you are pretending to be the person.

days.guide: Present the living museum to family. Give the unit test on a new biography.

questions.q: What is the author's purpose of a biography?
questions.a: To inform readers about a real person's life.

questions.q: What is the main topic of a biography?
questions.a: The person whose life it tells.

weeks.assessment_key: Research rubric (3 = proficient): 3 paragraphs (early life, big work, why we remember them) with accurate facts in own words; concluding sentence; poster with portrait, 5-event timeline in order, and a quote/fact box; speech in first person, audible, complete sentences. Unit test on the new biography: events sequenced correctly; main topic named; author's purpose = to inform about a real person's life.

weeks.prep: Get Volcanoes (Franklyn M. Branley, Let's-Read-and-Find-Out) and read it first. Gather clay (or play dough) around a small bottle, baking soda, vinegar, dish soap, red food coloring, and a tray. Print an earthquake passage and homophone pairs.
misconceptions: Thinking magma and lava are different materials. Both are melted rock — magma is underground; lava is magma that has come out.
Mixing up homophones (there/their). Their = belongs to them; there = a place.

days.guide: Read Volcanoes and study the diagram; label magma, crater, lava. Teach to/two/too and there/their.

questions.q: What is magma?
questions.a: Hot melted rock deep underground.

questions.q: What is lava?
questions.a: Magma that comes out of a volcano onto the surface.

days.guide: Find the point 'Volcanoes can build new land' and list the author's reasons. Write 'The author says ___ because ___.'

questions.q: What reasons support 'volcanoes can build new land'?
questions.a: The Hawaiian Islands were made by volcanoes, and the island of Surtsey rose from the sea near Iceland.

questions.q: Complete: The author says volcanoes build land because ___.
questions.a: lava cools and hardens into new rock, piling up into islands.

days.guide: Build a clay volcano and erupt it with baking soda and vinegar. Write 3 steps. Teach see/sea and right/write.

questions.q: Is the model eruption a real volcano?
questions.a: No — it is a chemical reaction making foam; a real eruption is melted rock from underground.

questions.q: Use 'sea' in a sentence.
questions.a: Example: Surtsey rose out of the sea.

days.guide: Read an earthquake passage; identify one point and two reasons. Use context to define 'fault' and 'plates.'

questions.q: What are plates?
questions.a: Giant pieces of Earth's crust that slowly move.

questions.q: What is a fault?
questions.a: A crack in Earth's crust where plates move past each other and earthquakes can happen.

days.guide: Complete a points-and-reasons organizer on a new passage and take the homophone quiz.

questions.q: Fix: 'Their are two volcanoes.'
questions.a: There are two volcanoes.

questions.q: Choose: I like to ___ (write/right) stories.
questions.a: write.

weeks.assessment_key: Point-and-reasons organizer: proficient states the author's point and 2 reasons from the passage (e.g., 'Volcanoes can build new land' — reasons: the Hawaiian Islands were built by volcanoes; the island of Surtsey rose out of the sea near Iceland in 1963). Homophone quiz (12): to/two/too, there/their, see/sea, right/write, know/no, hear/here — each used correctly in a sentence. Eruption steps: 1) put baking soda in the volcano 2) poured in vinegar 3) bubbly foam flowed out like lava.

weeks.prep: Get How Mountains Are Made (Kathleen Weidner Zoehfeld) and a second mountain text, plus a children's dictionary. Prepare 10 science words to alphabetize and two short rock passages for Friday.
misconceptions: Alphabetizing only by the first letter. When first letters match, look at the second letter (magma, mountain).
Comparing texts by listing only one text's facts. Use 'Both…' and 'Only…' sentence frames.

days.guide: Read How Mountains Are Made and list 4 important points about how mountains form. Use headings to find facts.

questions.q: Name one way mountains form.
questions.a: Plates of Earth's crust push together and fold or lift up the land (others: volcanoes, blocks lifted along faults).

questions.q: What wears mountains down over time?
questions.a: Wind, water, and ice (erosion).

days.guide: Read a second mountain text, list its points, and star the points that match.

questions.q: Why star matching points?
questions.a: To show which ideas both texts agree on.

questions.q: How do volcanoes make mountains?
questions.a: Lava erupts, cools, and piles up into a mountain.

days.guide: Complete the two-text chart and write 3 compound sentences comparing the texts.

questions.q: Complete: Both texts say ___, but only the second ___.
questions.a: Example: Both texts say plates push mountains up, but only the second tells about volcanoes.

questions.q: Which joining word shows a difference?
questions.a: but.

days.guide: Alphabetize 10 science words to the second letter and use guide words to look them up.

questions.q: Alphabetize: mountain, magma, lava.
questions.a: lava, magma, mountain.

questions.q: What are guide words?
questions.a: The words at the top of a dictionary page showing the first and last words on that page.

days.guide: Compare two rock passages in a chart, take an ABC-order quiz, and do a dictionary look-up.

questions.q: Would 'pebble' be on a page with guide words 'peach–pencil'?
questions.a: Yes — 'peb' comes after 'pea' and before 'pen.'

questions.q: Alphabetize: rock, river, rain.
questions.a: rain, river, rock.

weeks.assessment_key: Two-text chart: points that both texts share are starred; 3 compound sentences comparing (e.g., 'Both texts say plates push up mountains, but only the second explains erosion'). ABC-order quiz (suggested): crater, earth, fault, lava, magma, mountain, plate, rock, slope, volcano. Dictionary check: child uses guide words to find a word and copies its definition correctly.

weeks.prep: Gather a seed packet, a simple trail-mix recipe and ingredients (e.g., cereal, raisins, pretzels; check allergies), measuring cups, and paper. Make a list of 12 multisyllable science words (ingredient, measure, sprinkle, minute, seedling, gather, together, important, number, finally, carefully, container).
misconceptions: Skipping steps that seem obvious. Have someone follow the directions exactly to find missing steps.
Steps without numbers or time-order words. Number each step and start with first, next, then, last.

days.guide: Read steps on a seed packet and a recipe. Discuss why order matters and what happens if a step is skipped.

questions.q: What could happen if you skip 'water the seeds'?
questions.a: The seeds might not sprout.

questions.q: Why are steps numbered?
questions.a: To show the order to follow.

days.guide: Make trail mix following written steps, then rewrite the steps in your own words with numbers and time-order words.

questions.q: Write step 1 for trail mix.
questions.a: Example: First, pour one cup of cereal into a bowl.

questions.q: Split 'ingredient' into syllables.
questions.a: in-gre-di-ent.

days.guide: Choose something you know how to do and list the materials and steps.

questions.q: List steps for making a sandwich.
questions.a: Example: 1) Get two slices of bread. 2) Spread peanut butter. 3) Put the slices together. 4) Cut it in half.

questions.q: What goes in a materials list?
questions.a: Everything you need to do the task.

days.guide: Draft the how-to with introduction, numbered steps, and closing. A family member follows it exactly and notes missing steps.

questions.q: Why have someone follow your steps exactly?
questions.a: To find steps that are missing or unclear.

questions.q: Write a closing for a sandwich how-to.
questions.a: Example: Now enjoy your tasty sandwich!

days.guide: Revise after testing, add diagrams, and publish. Give the 12-word spelling check.

questions.q: Spell 'measure.'
questions.a: m-e-a-s-u-r-e.

questions.q: How does a diagram help a how-to?
questions.a: It shows what to do in a picture.

weeks.assessment_key: How-to rubric (3 = proficient): introduction tells what you will make or do; materials list; numbered steps in correct order with time-order words; a closing; a reader can follow it without help. Spelling (suggested 12): ingredient, measure, sprinkle, minute, seedling, gather, together, important, number, finally, carefully, container.

weeks.prep: Gather stationery, an envelope, and a stamp; have a relative's mailing address ready. Write a sample friendly letter to label and 5 informal sentences to rewrite. Prepare two short science texts with comparison questions for Friday.
misconceptions: Forgetting commas in the greeting and closing. 'Dear Grandma,' and 'Love,' always end with a comma.
Using slang in formal speech. Practice 'Hey, what's up?' → 'Hello, how are you?'

days.guide: Compare talking to a friend vs. a museum guide. Rewrite 5 informal sentences formally.

questions.q: Make formal: 'Hey, can I see that rock?'
questions.a: Excuse me, may I please see that rock?

questions.q: When do we use formal language?
questions.a: With adults we don't know well, in letters to businesses, and in presentations.

days.guide: Learn the 5 friendly-letter parts and label a sample letter.

questions.q: Name the 5 parts of a friendly letter.
questions.a: Date, greeting, body, closing, signature.

questions.q: Punctuate the greeting: Dear Grandpa
questions.a: Dear Grandpa,

days.guide: Write a letter to a relative about 3 things learned about volcanoes, mountains, or earthquakes, using science words.

questions.q: Write a body sentence with a science word.
questions.a: Example: I learned that magma is melted rock under the ground.

questions.q: Where does the closing go?
questions.a: After the body, before the signature (e.g., 'Love,').

days.guide: Edit the letter, address the envelope with capitals for city and state, and mail it. Read a nonfiction passage and log it.

questions.q: Capitalize: sacramento, california
questions.a: Sacramento, California.

questions.q: Where does the return address go?
questions.a: The top left corner of the envelope.

days.guide: Give the unit test: compare two science texts, find the author's reasons, and check letter format.

questions.q: Fix: 'your friend' as a closing.
questions.a: Your friend,

questions.q: What does 'reasons support a point' mean?
questions.a: The author gives facts that show the point is true.

weeks.assessment_key: Letter format rubric (3 = proficient): date, greeting with comma, body with 3 science facts using science words, closing with comma, signature; envelope with capitalized city and state. Unit test: questions comparing the two texts answered with details from both; the author's point and reasons identified; letter-format items correct (comma after greeting and closing).

weeks.prep: Get Winnie-the-Pooh (A. A. Milne, public domain in the U.S.) and preview chapters 1–3. Set up a book-club journal (chapter, characters, what happened, favorite part, question).
misconceptions: Describing characters without evidence ('Pooh is silly'). Add 'because in the story he…'
Missing the humor. Stop and ask 'Why is this funny?' — often the characters misunderstand something.

days.guide: Read Chapter 1. Describe Pooh's plan to get honey and why it fails. Start a book-club journal page.

questions.q: What is Pooh's plan to get honey?
questions.a: He rolls in mud to look like a small black rain cloud and floats up to the bees' tree holding a balloon.

questions.q: Why does the plan fail?
questions.a: The bees are suspicious, so Christopher Robin has to shoot the balloon with his popgun to bring Pooh down.

days.guide: Read Chapter 2 (Pooh gets stuck at Rabbit's). Discuss how Pooh and Rabbit each respond. Read Pooh's lines in his voice.

questions.q: Why does Pooh get stuck in Rabbit's door?
questions.a: He ate too much honey and condensed milk and became too fat to fit through.

questions.q: How does Rabbit respond?
questions.a: He is annoyed but makes the best of it — he uses Pooh's back legs as a towel-horse.

days.guide: Make a character-trait web for Pooh, Piglet, Rabbit, Owl, and Eeyore with text examples.

questions.q: Give a trait for Eeyore with evidence.
questions.a: Gloomy — he is always sad and expects bad things.

questions.q: Give a trait for Piglet.
questions.a: Small and nervous (timid) — he worries during the Woozle hunt.

days.guide: Read Chapter 3 (the Woozle hunt) and explain the joke. Discuss with a family member, taking turns and asking questions.

questions.q: What is the joke in the Woozle chapter?
questions.a: Pooh and Piglet are following their own footprints around the trees, so the 'Woozles' are really them.

questions.q: Who figures it out?
questions.a: Christopher Robin (and then Pooh realizes).

days.guide: The child answers written who/what/why questions on chapters 1–3 and does a one-minute fluency read.

questions.q: Who is Christopher Robin?
questions.a: The boy who is friends with Pooh and helps the animals.

questions.q: Why does Pooh want to climb the tree in Chapter 1?
questions.a: He hears buzzing and wants honey.

weeks.assessment_key: Journal entries: one per chapter with characters, main event, and a question. Written comprehension (model): Ch. 1 — Pooh tries to get honey from the bees by floating up with a balloon while covered in mud to look like a little black rain cloud; it fails because the bees are suspicious, and Christopher Robin shoots the balloon to get him down. Ch. 2 — Pooh eats so much honey and condensed milk at Rabbit's house that he gets stuck in the doorway for a week until he is thin enough to be pulled out. Ch. 3 — Pooh and Piglet follow tracks around a spinney, but the tracks are their own. Fluency: record WCPM.

weeks.prep: Preview Winnie-the-Pooh chapters 4 and 6. Gather sticky notes, a story-structure chart (beginning/problem, middle, ending/solution), and a list of 30 irregular words (said, laugh, enough, friend, people, because, again, any, many, does, though, through, eye, four, …).
misconceptions: Thinking point of view means the narrator only. Ask how each character felt about the same event.
Sounding out irregular words letter by letter. Practice them as whole words by sight.

days.guide: Read Chapter 4 (Eeyore loses a tail). Discuss how the beginning introduces the problem and the ending solves it.

questions.q: Where is Eeyore's tail?
questions.a: Owl is using it as a bell-pull on his door.

questions.q: How is the problem solved?
questions.a: Pooh brings it back and Christopher Robin nails it back on Eeyore.

days.guide: Read Chapter 6 (Eeyore's birthday). Tell the gift story from Piglet's view, then Eeyore's.

questions.q: What happens to Pooh's gift?
questions.a: He eats the honey on the way, so he gives Eeyore the empty pot — a 'Useful Pot to Keep Things In.'

questions.q: What happens to Piglet's balloon, and how does Eeyore feel?
questions.a: Piglet falls and pops it; Eeyore is happy because the burst balloon fits in and out of the pot.

days.guide: Review 30 irregular words with a speed-read game and a spelling self-check.

questions.q: Spell 'friend' and 'because.'
questions.a: f-r-i-e-n-d; b-e-c-a-u-s-e.

questions.q: Which part of 'said' is irregular?
questions.a: The ai says short e.

days.guide: Perform a scene from Eeyore's birthday with voices for Pooh, Piglet, and Eeyore.

questions.q: How should Eeyore's voice sound?
questions.a: Slow, low, and gloomy.

questions.q: How should Piglet sound after popping the balloon?
questions.a: Worried and sorry.

days.guide: The child fills a story-structure chart for one chapter and writes a paragraph on how two characters felt differently about the same event.

questions.q: How did Pooh and Eeyore feel about the empty honey pot?
questions.a: Pooh felt a little embarrassed about eating the honey; Eeyore was delighted with a useful pot.

questions.q: What does a story ending do?
questions.a: Solves the problem and wraps up the story.

weeks.assessment_key: Story-structure chart (Chapter 4): Beginning — Eeyore has lost his tail; Middle — Pooh searches and visits Owl; Ending — Pooh sees Owl's bell-pull is Eeyore's tail, and Christopher Robin nails it back on. Point-of-view paragraph (Eeyore's birthday): Piglet feels upset and embarrassed that he popped the balloon; Eeyore is pleased because he can put the burst balloon in and out of his Useful Pot. Rubric 3 = both characters' feelings explained with evidence. Reader's theater: different voices, fluent reading.

weeks.prep: Preview Winnie-the-Pooh Chapter 10. Gather favorite books from the year and a computer or tablet for typing. Write 20 review spelling words from the year (said, friend, because, people, rain, beach, boat, night, bird, turn, happy, sky, unhappy, helpful, didn't, little, write, right, there, their).
misconceptions: Book reviews that retell the whole story, including the ending. Summarize the beginning only — no spoilers.
Reasons that are just opinions repeated. Each reason should point to something in the book.

days.guide: Read Chapter 10 (the party for Pooh). Discuss how the book ends. Rate the book with stars and give a reason.

questions.q: Why does Christopher Robin give a party?
questions.a: To honor Pooh for his clever idea to rescue Piglet during the flood.

questions.q: What gift does Pooh get?
questions.a: A special pencil case with pencils.

days.guide: Choose the favorite book of the year and plan a review: summary without spoilers, opinion, 3 reasons, recommendation.

questions.q: What is a spoiler?
questions.a: Telling the ending or a surprise.

questions.q: Give a recommendation sentence.
questions.a: Example: Kids who love funny animals will enjoy this book.

days.guide: Draft the review with linking words and at least 4 describing words.

questions.q: Give 2 describing words for Frog and Toad.
questions.a: Examples: funny, kind, cozy.

questions.q: Name linking words for reasons.
questions.a: because, also, another reason.

days.guide: Type the review with help, add a cover picture, and print or share it.

questions.q: Which key makes a capital letter?
questions.a: The Shift key.

questions.q: Why add a cover picture?
questions.a: So readers know which book it is.

days.guide: Read the review aloud and listen to a family member's; give the 20-word spelling test.

questions.q: Spell 'people.'
questions.a: p-e-o-p-l-e.

questions.q: Spell 'their' (belongs to them).
questions.a: t-h-e-i-r.

weeks.assessment_key: Book review rubric (3 = proficient): short summary without the ending; clear opinion; 3 reasons with examples; linking words; recommendation ('Readers who like… will enjoy this'). Cumulative spelling test of 20 words: 17+ proficient.

weeks.prep: Choose an on-level end-of-year fluency passage with 4–5 comprehension questions. Prepare the phonics/spelling inventory (vowel teams, r-controlled, prefixes/suffixes, two-syllable words, irregular words). Gather the year's writing portfolio and a summer reading list template.
misconceptions: Picking portfolio pieces by neatness only. Choose pieces that show growth and different kinds of writing.
Setting a vague summer goal ('read a lot'). Make it measurable: '10 books' or '20 minutes a day.'

days.guide: The child reads an on-level passage for one minute and answers comprehension questions. Compare with fall and mid-year scores.

questions.q: How do you find WCPM?
questions.a: Count words read in one minute and subtract errors.

questions.q: Why compare to fall?
questions.a: To see how much reading has grown.

days.guide: Give the phonics and spelling inventory and the irregular-word reading check.

questions.q: Spell 'unhappy.'
questions.a: u-n-h-a-p-p-y.

questions.q: Spell 'night.'
questions.a: n-i-g-h-t.

days.guide: Choose 5 best pieces (narrative, fable, report, opinion, poem) and write a one-sentence reflection for each.

questions.q: Write a reflection sentence for a fable.
questions.a: Example: My fable shows I learned to end a story with a clear lesson.

questions.q: Why include different kinds of writing?
questions.a: To show all the kinds of writing you learned.

days.guide: Present the portfolio to family, reading one favorite piece aloud and explaining one way you grew as a writer.

questions.q: Give an example of growth.
questions.a: Example: I now use temporal words and details in my stories.

questions.q: What makes a good presentation?
questions.a: Clear voice, eye contact, and answering questions.

days.guide: Make a summer reading list of 10 books and set a reading goal. Celebrate the year.

questions.q: Name a series to add to the list.
questions.a: Examples: Frog and Toad, Henry and Mudge, Magic Tree House.

questions.q: Write a measurable reading goal.
questions.a: Example: I will read 20 minutes every day this summer.

weeks.assessment_key: Fluency: record WCPM and compare to fall and mid-year (end-of-grade-2 goal about 90–100 WCPM). Comprehension: 4/5 correct. Phonics inventory: record correct/incorrect for vowel teams (rain, play, tree, beach, boat, snow, night), r-controlled (car, corn, her, bird, turn), prefixes/suffixes (unhappy, reread, helpful, quickly), two-syllable words (paper, raincoat), and irregular words (said, friend, because, people). Portfolio: 5 pieces with one-sentence reflections; presentation explains one way the child grew.

HEALTH.overview: Health 2 lessons are short (about 20-30 minutes) and practical: read or discuss, model the skill, have your child practice through role-play, an experiment, or a tracker, then check by asking them to show or explain it. Keep trackers and logs on the fridge so habits continue through the week, and collect work in a health portfolio for weeks 35-36. Preview the sensitive weeks ahead of time (bullying in week 4, body safety in week 28, weapons and online safety in week 29, medicines, poisons, tobacco and alcohol in weeks 30-32) and use calm, simple, matter-of-fact language.

weeks.prep: 'In My Heart: A Book of Feelings' by Jo Witek (library), paper for a feelings thermometer, index cards for the anger-sort (yelling, hitting, talking, drawing, walking away, taking deep breaths, throwing things).
misconceptions: Thinking some feelings are bad: all feelings are okay; what we DO with them can be healthy or unhealthy.
Thinking everyone feels the same way about an event: people can feel differently about the same thing.

days.guide: Read 'In My Heart.' Stop on each page and have your child name the feeling and point to clues in the pictures. List every feeling word together.

questions.q: Name three feelings from the book.
questions.a: Any three named in the book, e.g., happy, sad, brave, angry, scared, calm, hopeful, shy.

questions.q: What is an emotion?
questions.a: A feeling, like happy, sad, angry or proud.

days.guide: Draw a thermometer from 'calm' (bottom) to 'very upset' (top); your child colors today's level and tells why.

questions.q: What does the top of the thermometer mean?
questions.a: Very upset (big feelings).

questions.q: Where are you today and why?
questions.a: Child names a level with a reason.

days.guide: Discuss how two people could feel differently about a thunderstorm or a new baby.

questions.q: How might two people feel about a thunderstorm?
questions.a: One might feel scared, another excited or cozy.

questions.q: Is it okay to feel differently from someone else?
questions.a: Yes; people can feel different ways about the same event.

days.guide: Sort cards of ways to show anger into healthy and unhealthy.

questions.q: Is hitting a healthy way to show anger?
questions.a: No, it hurts others.

questions.q: Name a healthy way to show anger.
questions.a: Talk about it, draw it, walk away, take deep breaths.

days.guide: Write 3 sentences: 'I feel ___ when ___. I can ___.'

questions.q: What does 'frustrated' mean?
questions.a: Upset because something is hard or not working.

questions.q: What does 'proud' mean?
questions.a: Feeling good about something you did.

weeks.assessment_key: Sort key: healthy = talking about it, drawing, walking away to calm down, deep breaths; unhealthy = yelling, hitting, throwing things. Sentences: 3 complete 'I feel ___ when ___. I can ___.' with a real feeling word, a matching situation, and a healthy action (e.g., 'I feel frustrated when my tower falls. I can take three deep breaths and try again.'). Proficient = sort all correct + 3 sentences with healthy actions.

weeks.prep: Jar with lid, water, glitter glue or clear glue and glitter (adult seals lid with glue), pillow, book, feelings chart; GoNoodle Flow or kids yoga video.
misconceptions: Thinking calming down means hiding feelings: calming helps you think so you can solve the problem.
Breathing fast when trying to calm down: slow, deep belly breaths work best.

days.guide: Model balloon breathing (slowly fill your belly like a balloon, let it out), five-finger breathing (trace up a finger breathing in, down breathing out), and counting to 10.

questions.q: How do you do five-finger breathing?
questions.a: Trace up each finger while breathing in and down while breathing out.

questions.q: Why do slow breaths help?
questions.a: They slow your heart and body so you feel calmer.

days.guide: Make a glitter calm-down jar; shake it and breathe slowly as glitter settles.

questions.q: How is the jar like your feelings?
questions.a: When upset, thoughts swirl like glitter; when you calm down, they settle.

days.guide: Set up a calm corner with a pillow, book and feelings chart; agree on how to use it.

questions.q: When can you use the calm corner?
questions.a: When you have a big feeling and need to calm down.

days.guide: Do a GoNoodle Flow or yoga video; notice how your body feels.

questions.q: How did your body feel after?
questions.a: Answers like relaxed, slower breathing, calmer.

days.guide: Role-play losing a game and use one calming strategy.

questions.q: What is stress?
questions.a: A worried or pressured feeling when something is hard.

weeks.assessment_key: Role-play: in a pretend frustrating moment (losing a game), child names the feeling, uses one strategy correctly (balloon breathing, five-finger breathing, counting to 10, calm-down jar, calm corner), then says a calm next step ('Good game, can we play again?'). Proficient = all three parts.

weeks.prep: 'The Invisible Boy' by Trudy Ludwig (library), paper.
misconceptions: Thinking 'being nice' means saying yes to everything: good friends are kind but can disagree respectfully.
Blaming in a conflict ('You always…'): use an I-message that tells how you feel.

days.guide: Read 'The Invisible Boy'; discuss how Brian felt left out.

questions.q: Why did Brian feel invisible?
questions.a: Other kids didn't notice him or include him (not picked for games, not invited to a party).

questions.q: What changed for Brian?
questions.a: New student Justin was friends with him and included him, and Brian became 'colorful.'

days.guide: Write a 'Recipe for a Good Friend.'

questions.q: Name two ingredients of a good friend.
questions.a: Kindness, sharing, listening, including others, honesty.

days.guide: Practice active listening: eyes on speaker, nod, ask a question.

questions.q: What are three active listening moves?
questions.a: Look at the speaker, nod, ask a question.

days.guide: Teach 'I feel ___ when ___ because ___'; do 3 role-plays.

questions.q: Make an I-message for 'a friend grabbed my toy.'
questions.a: 'I feel upset when you grab my toy because I was still using it.'

days.guide: Name 3 qualities of a good friend; show an I-message.

questions.q: What is empathy?
questions.a: Understanding and caring about how someone else feels.

weeks.assessment_key: Friend recipe lists at least 4 ingredients (kindness, sharing, listening, including others, honesty, taking turns). Role-play: correct I-message, e.g., 'I feel left out when you don't let me play because I want to be part of the game.' Three qualities named. Proficient = 4+ ingredients + complete I-message.

weeks.prep: 'Stand Tall, Molly Lou Melon' by Patty Lovell (library); paper to trace a hand. Preview: talk calmly, and invite your child to share any experiences.
misconceptions: Calling every mean moment 'bullying': bullying is on purpose, repeated, and hurtful (often with a power difference).
Thinking telling an adult is tattling: telling to keep someone safe is reporting, not tattling.

days.guide: Read 'Stand Tall, Molly Lou Melon'; talk about how Molly handled teasing.

questions.q: How did Molly Lou handle Ronald's teasing?
questions.a: She remembered her grandma's advice, believed in herself, and proudly showed what she could do.

questions.q: Who gave Molly good advice?
questions.a: Her grandma.

days.guide: Explain rude (accidental, once), mean (on purpose, once), bullying (on purpose, repeated, hurtful).

questions.q: What three things make something bullying?
questions.a: On purpose, repeated, and hurtful.

days.guide: Practice upstander moves: say 'Stop,' walk away with the target, tell a trusted adult.

questions.q: What is an upstander?
questions.a: Someone who helps when they see bullying.

questions.q: What is a bystander?
questions.a: Someone who sees it but does nothing.

days.guide: Trace a hand; write one trusted adult on each finger.

questions.q: Who is a trusted adult?
questions.a: A grown-up who keeps you safe and listens, like a parent, grandparent, teacher, coach.

days.guide: Respond to 3 scenarios; explain telling vs. tattling.

questions.q: What's the difference between telling and tattling?
questions.a: Telling helps keep someone safe; tattling is trying to get someone in trouble.

weeks.assessment_key: Scenario responses (examples): 1) A kid calls a classmate names every day: say 'Stop,' stand with/walk away with the target, tell a trusted adult. 2) Someone is pushed off the swing again and again: help the person leave and tell an adult. 3) You are left out on purpose repeatedly: tell a trusted adult and find kind friends. Telling vs. tattling: telling helps someone who is hurt or unsafe; tattling just tries to get someone in trouble. Proficient = correct upstander actions in all 3 + accurate difference.

weeks.prep: Family photos; 'The Family Book' by Todd Parr (library); paper for a chore chart.
misconceptions: Thinking there is one 'right' kind of family: families come in many shapes and sizes.
Thinking chores are only adults' jobs: everyone can help the family.

days.guide: Read 'The Family Book'; list ways families are alike and different.

questions.q: How are families different?
questions.a: Some are big or small, have one parent or two, two moms or two dads, are adopted, live with grandparents, etc.

questions.q: How are all families alike in the book?
questions.a: They love each other, help each other and like to be together.

days.guide: Draw your family and label how each person helps.

questions.q: How does one person in your family help?
questions.a: Specific job.

days.guide: Make a chore chart; choose two jobs.

questions.q: What does responsibility mean?
questions.a: Doing the jobs you are supposed to do.

days.guide: Hold a short family meeting to share feelings and plan a fun activity.

questions.q: Why have family meetings?
questions.a: To share feelings, solve problems, and plan together.

days.guide: Tell 3 ways your family supports you and 2 ways you support them.

questions.q: What does 'support' mean?
questions.a: Helping and caring for someone.

weeks.assessment_key: Family portrait: each person drawn and labeled with a way they help. Oral: 3 ways family supports the child (e.g., cooks meals, helps with homework, hugs when sad) and 2 ways the child helps (sets the table, feeds the pet). Proficient = all labeled + 5 specific examples.

weeks.prep: Lotion, glitter, soap, timer, a plate of water and ground pepper, dish soap.
misconceptions: Thinking a quick rinse is enough: scrub with soap for at least 20 seconds.
Coughing into hands: cough or sneeze into your elbow so germs don't go onto hands.

days.guide: Put lotion and glitter on your hand; shake hands with family; see how 'germs' spread.

questions.q: What are germs?
questions.a: Tiny living things (like bacteria and viruses) that can make you sick.

questions.q: How did the glitter show germs spreading?
questions.a: It moved from hand to hand when we touched.

days.guide: Teach 5 steps: wet, lather, scrub 20 seconds, rinse, dry; hum 'Happy Birthday' twice.

questions.q: How long should you scrub?
questions.a: At least 20 seconds (Happy Birthday twice).

days.guide: Sprinkle pepper on water; touch with a soapy finger; pepper rushes away.

questions.q: What happened to the pepper?
questions.a: It moved away from the soapy finger.

questions.q: What does this show?
questions.a: Soap helps push away and remove germs.

days.guide: Practice coughing and sneezing into an elbow; explain vaccines help the body learn to fight certain germs.

questions.q: Why sneeze into your elbow?
questions.a: So germs don't spread to your hands and then to other people.

questions.q: How do vaccines help?
questions.a: They teach your body to fight certain germs so you don't get as sick.

days.guide: Demonstrate handwashing; list 3 times to wash.

questions.q: Name 3 times to wash hands.
questions.a: Before eating, after the bathroom, after sneezing/coughing (also after playing outside or with pets).

weeks.assessment_key: Handwashing checklist: wet hands; lather with soap; scrub at least 20 seconds (backs, between fingers, under nails); rinse; dry with a clean towel. Times to wash (any 3): before eating, after using the bathroom, after coughing/sneezing/blowing nose, after playing outside, after touching pets, before helping cook. Proficient = all 5 steps + 3 times.

weeks.prep: Mirror, toothbrush, floss; 3 hard-boiled eggs, cups of water, soda and vinegar (start Day 2 and leave overnight).
misconceptions: Brushing for only a few seconds: brush 2 minutes, twice a day.
Thinking only candy causes cavities: sugary drinks and sticky snacks also feed plaque bacteria.

days.guide: Teach enamel (hard outer layer) and gums; plaque (sticky germ film) makes acid that causes cavities. Count teeth in a mirror.

questions.q: What is plaque?
questions.a: A sticky film of germs on teeth that can cause cavities.

questions.q: What is enamel?
questions.a: The hard outer covering of a tooth.

days.guide: Soak eggs overnight in water, soda and vinegar; predict what will happen.

questions.q: What does the eggshell stand for?
questions.a: Tooth enamel.

days.guide: Observe and record the eggs; discuss limiting sugary drinks.

questions.q: What happened to the egg in vinegar?
questions.a: It bubbled and the shell got soft or dissolved.

questions.q: What happened to the egg in soda?
questions.a: It turned brown/stained.

days.guide: Practice 2-minute brushing in small circles and flossing; start a brushing chart.

questions.q: How long and how often should you brush?
questions.a: 2 minutes, twice a day.

questions.q: Why floss?
questions.a: To clean between teeth where a brush can't reach.

days.guide: Explain egg results; demonstrate brushing.

questions.q: What is a cavity?
questions.a: A hole in a tooth caused by decay.

weeks.assessment_key: Experiment record: water egg - little or no change; soda egg - stained brown, shell may feel softer; vinegar egg - bubbles formed, shell softened or dissolved. Conclusion: acidic and sugary drinks can stain and weaken enamel, like eggshells. Brushing demo: small circles on all surfaces, along gums, 2 minutes, plus flossing between teeth. Proficient = accurate results + correct brushing.

weeks.prep: Sleep log (4 nights: bedtime, wake time), paper and crayons.
misconceptions: Thinking kids need the same sleep as adults: children ages 6-12 need 9-12 hours.
Thinking screens help you fall asleep: bright screens and exciting content make it harder.

days.guide: Explain kids need 9-12 hours; sleep helps the brain learn, the body grow, and you feel good.

questions.q: How many hours of sleep do kids your age need?
questions.a: 9 to 12 hours.

questions.q: Name one way sleep helps.
questions.a: Helps your brain remember, your body grow and heal, and gives energy.

days.guide: Start the 4-night sleep log.

questions.q: If you sleep from 8:00 p.m. to 6:30 a.m., how long is that?
questions.a: 10 and a half hours.

days.guide: Draw a calm bedtime routine: bath, teeth, book, lights out.

questions.q: What is a routine?
questions.a: Steps you do in the same order every day.

days.guide: Discuss screens before bed; set a family 'screens off' time (about 1 hour before bed).

questions.q: Why turn off screens before bed?
questions.a: Bright light and exciting shows keep your brain awake.

days.guide: Total sleep hours; set a bedtime goal.

questions.q: What is your bedtime goal?
questions.a: Specific time.

weeks.assessment_key: Sleep log: 4 nights with bedtime, wake time and hours (e.g., 8:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m. = 11 hours). Total and average correct. Bedtime goal is specific (e.g., 'lights out by 8:00'). Proficient = accurate totals + specific goal.

weeks.prep: Dark construction paper and small objects (leave in sun Day 1), sunscreen bottle, sunglasses, hat; UV beads optional.
misconceptions: Thinking you only need sunscreen on hot days: UV rays reach you on cloudy and cool days too.
Thinking loud noise only hurts for a moment: repeated loud sounds can cause permanent hearing loss.

days.guide: Leave paper with objects in the sun; later see faded areas; discuss skin.

questions.q: Why did the paper fade except under the objects?
questions.a: UV rays from the sun faded the uncovered paper.

questions.q: What do UV rays do to skin?
questions.a: They can cause sunburn and skin damage.

days.guide: Teach 'Slip, Slop, Slap, Wrap'; read the SPF on a label.

questions.q: What do Slip, Slop, Slap, Wrap mean?
questions.a: Slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen, slap on a hat, wrap on sunglasses.

questions.q: What does SPF tell you?
questions.a: How well sunscreen protects against sunburn (30 or higher recommended).

days.guide: Discuss goggles, never looking at the sun, and the 20-20-20 rule.

questions.q: What is the 20-20-20 rule?
questions.a: Every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds.

days.guide: Compare quiet and loud sounds; discuss protecting hearing.

questions.q: How can you protect your ears?
questions.a: Turn volume down, wear earplugs/earmuffs, move away from loud noise.

days.guide: Make a poster about protecting skin, eyes and ears.

questions.q: Give one tip for each.
questions.a: Skin: sunscreen; eyes: sunglasses; ears: lower the volume.

weeks.assessment_key: Poster has at least one correct tip for each: skin (sunscreen SPF 30+, reapply every 2 hours, shirt, hat, shade), eyes (sunglasses, never look at the sun, goggles for projects, 20-20-20 screen breaks), ears (turn volume down, earplugs or earmuffs for loud places, step away from loud noise). Proficient = 3 accurate tips with pictures.

weeks.prep: Goal chart, stickers; travel soap, tissues, toothbrush for a hygiene kit.
misconceptions: Making goals too big or vague ('be healthy'): make them specific ('brush twice a day').
Giving up after a missed day: just start again the next day.

days.guide: Review unit habits; rate each with a smiley scale.

questions.q: Which habit are you best at?
questions.a: Child names one.

days.guide: Choose one habit to improve; write it as a goal.

questions.q: What is a goal?
questions.a: Something you plan and work to do.

days.guide: Make a 2-week sticker tracker.

questions.q: Why track a habit?
questions.a: To see progress and remember to do it.

days.guide: Pack a hygiene kit; explain each item.

questions.q: Why carry travel soap?
questions.a: To wash hands and remove germs when away from home.

days.guide: Give the 10-question oral quiz; begin tracking.

questions.q: What is a habit?
questions.a: Something you do so often it becomes automatic.

weeks.assessment_key: Oral quiz (10): 1) Germs are tiny living things that can make you sick. 2) Scrub hands at least 20 seconds. 3) Sneeze into your elbow. 4) Brush 2 minutes, twice a day. 5) Plaque is a sticky germ film that causes cavities. 6) Floss cleans between teeth. 7) Kids need 9-12 hours of sleep. 8) Turn off screens about an hour before bed. 9) Slip, slop, slap, wrap protects skin and eyes. 10) Use SPF 30+ sunscreen and reapply. Proficient = 8/10 + a specific goal with tracker started.

weeks.prep: MyPlate printable (myplate.gov), grocery flyers, scissors, glue; 15 food cards.
misconceptions: Thinking cheese is protein: on MyPlate, cheese is in dairy (beans and eggs are protein).
Thinking potatoes and corn are grains: potatoes are vegetables; corn kernels count as a vegetable (cornmeal/popcorn are grains).

days.guide: Teach the 5 MyPlate groups; name 3 foods for each.

questions.q: Name the 5 food groups.
questions.a: Fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy.

questions.q: Which group is yogurt?
questions.a: Dairy.

days.guide: Cut foods from flyers; glue onto MyPlate.

questions.q: Where do beans go?
questions.a: Protein (they can also count as vegetables).

days.guide: Draw your dinner; check groups present and missing.

questions.q: Which group was missing from your dinner?
questions.a: Child identifies.

days.guide: Play food group freeze.

questions.q: Which group is rice?
questions.a: Grains.

days.guide: Sort 15 cards; plan a balanced lunch.

questions.q: Which part of MyPlate is about half the plate?
questions.a: Fruits and vegetables together make about half.

weeks.assessment_key: Food sort (example 15): Fruits - apple, banana, orange; Vegetables - carrot, broccoli, potato; Grains - bread, rice, oatmeal; Protein - chicken, eggs, beans; Dairy - milk, yogurt, cheese. Balanced lunch includes all 5 groups (e.g., turkey sandwich on whole-wheat bread, carrots, apple, milk). Proficient = 13+/15 + balanced lunch.

weeks.prep: A variety of fruits and vegetables (one new to taste), cups, measuring teaspoon, sugar; labels from juice, soda, milk.
misconceptions: Thinking juice is as healthy as whole fruit: whole fruit has fiber and usually less sugar per serving.
Thinking you only need water when thirsty: drink water throughout the day.

days.guide: Make a color chart of produce; taste a new one.

questions.q: Why 'eat the rainbow'?
questions.a: Different colored foods give different vitamins and nutrients.

days.guide: Sort vegetables by plant part: carrot (root), celery (stem), lettuce/spinach (leaf), peas/corn (seed), tomato/cucumber (fruit), broccoli (flower).

questions.q: What part of the plant is a carrot?
questions.a: Root.

questions.q: What part is celery?
questions.a: Stem.

days.guide: Learn why the body needs water; track cups today.

questions.q: Why does your body need water?
questions.a: To stay cool, move nutrients, help digestion and keep every part working.

days.guide: Measure sugar: 12-oz soda about 10 teaspoons; 8-oz apple juice about 6; 8-oz plain milk about 3 (natural milk sugar). Use labels: about 4 grams = 1 teaspoon.

questions.q: Which drink had the most sugar?
questions.a: Soda.

questions.q: If a label says 24 grams of sugar, about how many teaspoons?
questions.a: About 6 teaspoons (24 ÷ 4).

days.guide: Write 3 reasons to eat produce and drink water.

questions.q: What is a nutrient?
questions.a: Something in food your body needs to grow and stay healthy.

weeks.assessment_key: Three reasons (any accurate): fruits and vegetables give vitamins and minerals; they give fiber that helps digestion; they help your body grow and fight sickness; water keeps the body cool, carries nutrients, and helps every part work. Rainbow chart has a fruit/vegetable for each color. Proficient = 3 accurate reasons + complete chart.

weeks.prep: Snack foods or pictures; paper for a decision-making worksheet; ingredients for apple 'nachos' (apple slices, peanut/seed butter, raisins) or veggie wraps.
misconceptions: Thinking all snacks are unhealthy: snacks can be healthy fuel.
Thinking 'whoa' foods are 'bad': they're for once in a while, not every day.

days.guide: Explain breakfast fuels the brain; plan 3 balanced breakfasts.

questions.q: Why is breakfast important?
questions.a: It gives your brain and body energy to start the day.

questions.q: Give a balanced breakfast.
questions.a: Oatmeal with fruit and milk; eggs, whole-wheat toast and orange slices.

days.guide: Sort snacks into go (every day: fruit, veggies, plain yogurt), slow (sometimes: granola bar, pretzels), whoa (once in a while: candy, chips, soda).

questions.q: Is an apple a go, slow or whoa food?
questions.a: Go.

questions.q: Is soda go, slow or whoa?
questions.a: Whoa.

days.guide: Use 3 steps (list choices, think about results, choose) to pick a snack.

questions.q: What are the 3 decision steps?
questions.a: List choices, think about what will happen, choose the best one.

days.guide: Wash produce; make apple nachos or veggie wraps.

questions.q: Why wash produce?
questions.a: To remove dirt and germs.

days.guide: Explain your snack choice with the steps.

questions.q: What is added sugar?
questions.a: Sugar put into foods when they're made, not naturally in them.

weeks.assessment_key: Decision worksheet: Step 1 choices listed (e.g., chips, apple with cheese, cookie); Step 2 results thought through (energy, sugar crash, fullness); Step 3 choice with reason ('apple and cheese because it gives energy and has fruit and dairy'). Proficient = all steps with a health-based reason.

weeks.prep: 3 cereal boxes with Nutrition Facts labels; food ads (TV, magazines, boxes); paper and markers.
misconceptions: Comparing sugar without checking serving size: compare the same serving amounts.
Believing everything an ad says: ads are made to sell.

days.guide: Find serving size and sugar on 3 cereals.

questions.q: Where do you find sugar on a box?
questions.a: On the Nutrition Facts label (Total Sugars / Added Sugars).

days.guide: Rank cereals by sugar per serving.

questions.q: If one cereal has 4 g sugar and another 12 g, which has less?
questions.a: The 4 g one.

days.guide: Look at food ads; identify tricks.

questions.q: Name an ad trick.
questions.a: Cartoon characters, free toys, bright colors, catchy songs, famous people.

days.guide: Design a healthy food ad with honest claims.

questions.q: What is an honest claim?
questions.a: A true statement, like 'has 5 grams of fiber.'

days.guide: Explain how ads influence kids and how labels help.

questions.q: What does 'influence' mean?
questions.a: To affect what someone thinks or does.

weeks.assessment_key: Label comparison: serving size and grams of sugar recorded for 3 cereals, ranked least to most correctly. Ad design: honest claims, healthy food. Explanation: ads use tricks (cartoon characters, toys, bright colors, celebrities, catchy songs) to make kids want products; labels give real facts like sugar and serving size. Proficient = correct ranking + 2 ad tricks + label use.

weeks.prep: Local produce; 'From Seed to Plant' by Gail Gibbons (library); a cup, soil and lettuce or herb seeds.
misconceptions: Thinking food comes from the store: it comes from farms and travels to stores.
Thinking all foods grow all year: many are seasonal.

days.guide: Trace a food from a California farm to the table; draw the steps.

questions.q: What happens after strawberries are picked?
questions.a: They are packed, cooled, and trucked to stores.

days.guide: Visit a farmers market or produce section; list 5 local foods.

questions.q: What is a producer?
questions.a: Someone who grows or makes food or goods, like a farmer.

days.guide: Learn California seasons: spring strawberries, asparagus; summer peaches, tomatoes, corn; fall apples, grapes, pumpkins; winter oranges and citrus, broccoli.

questions.q: Name a fruit that grows in California in winter.
questions.a: Oranges (citrus).

days.guide: Plant herbs or lettuce seeds in a cup.

questions.q: What does a seed need to grow?
questions.a: Water, light, air and soil (nutrients).

days.guide: Explain the farm-to-table path for one food.

questions.q: Who are the helpers along the way?
questions.a: Farmers, workers, truck drivers, store workers.

weeks.assessment_key: Farm-to-table drawing, e.g., strawberries: planted and grown on a California farm, picked by farmworkers, packed and cooled, trucked to a store or market, bought, washed, eaten. Proficient = 5+ correct steps in order.

weeks.prep: Kitchen, fridge thermometer, recipe card.
misconceptions: Using the same cutting board for raw meat and veggies: keep them separate.
Leaving food out a long time: chill leftovers within 2 hours.

days.guide: Teach Clean, Separate, Cook, Chill; find examples.

questions.q: What are the 4 food safety steps?
questions.a: Clean, separate, cook, chill.

questions.q: What is cross-contamination?
questions.a: Germs moving from one food (like raw meat) to another.

days.guide: Check fridge temperature with a parent.

questions.q: How cold should the fridge be?
questions.a: 40°F or colder.

days.guide: Plan a balanced dinner using MyPlate.

questions.q: Does your meal have all 5 groups?
questions.a: Checks plan.

days.guide: Help cook, washing hands and produce first.

questions.q: Why wash hands before cooking?
questions.a: To keep germs out of the food.

days.guide: Give the nutrition unit quiz.

questions.q: Where should raw meat go in the fridge?
questions.a: On the bottom shelf, so juices can't drip on other foods.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit quiz (sample answers): 5 food groups = fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy; go/slow/whoa examples correct; serving size must be checked before comparing; ads use tricks; food safety steps = clean, separate, cook, chill; fridge at 40°F or colder. Proficient = 80% correct.

weeks.prep: Activity log, timer; ideas list.
misconceptions: Thinking only sports count: walking, dancing, playing and biking all count.
Thinking activity must happen all at once: minutes can add up throughout the day.

days.guide: Teach kids need 60 minutes of activity daily; brainstorm activities.

questions.q: How many minutes of activity do kids need each day?
questions.a: 60 minutes.

days.guide: Rate mood before and after a 10-minute walk.

questions.q: How does activity affect mood?
questions.a: It usually makes you feel happier and calmer.

days.guide: Start a week-long activity log.

questions.q: If you played 20 minutes before lunch and 40 after, total?
questions.a: 60 minutes.

days.guide: Plan a family active challenge.

questions.q: Name an activity the whole family can do.
questions.a: Bike ride, hike, dance party.

days.guide: Total minutes; set next week's goal.

questions.q: How does activity give you energy?
questions.a: It strengthens your heart and muscles so your body works better.

weeks.assessment_key: Activity log: daily minutes for a week, total correct (e.g., 45 + 60 + 30 + 70 + 50 + 65 + 40 = 360 minutes). Goal is specific (e.g., 60 minutes on at least 5 days). Proficient = log complete + accurate total + goal.

weeks.prep: Activity log, timer, list paper.
misconceptions: Thinking screens are always bad: balance matters.
Counting screen time with active games as active: sitting games are sedentary.

days.guide: Track screen time 2 days; compare with active minutes.

questions.q: Which was more: screen or active minutes?
questions.a: Child compares from data.

days.guide: List 10 active swaps for screen time.

questions.q: Give an active swap.
questions.a: Ride a bike instead of watching a show.

days.guide: Plan and enjoy a screen-free afternoon outdoors.

questions.q: What does sedentary mean?
questions.a: Sitting still, not moving much.

days.guide: Check last week's goal; update the log.

questions.q: Did you meet your goal?
questions.a: Uses numbers from log.

days.guide: Explain how balance helps health.

questions.q: Why balance screens with movement?
questions.a: Moving keeps your body strong and helps you sleep and feel good.

weeks.assessment_key: Goal progress compared with week 17 goal (met/not met with numbers). Explanation: balancing screens with movement keeps heart, muscles and bones strong, helps sleep and mood; too much sitting (sedentary time) can make you tired and less healthy. Proficient = accurate progress + explanation.

weeks.prep: Paper skeleton template, brads, scissors; optional cleaned chicken bone.
misconceptions: Thinking bones are dead and dry: living bones grow and repair.
Thinking muscles push: muscles only pull; pairs work together (biceps bends, triceps straightens).

days.guide: Teach skull, ribs, spine and their jobs; feel them.

questions.q: What does the skull protect?
questions.a: The brain.

questions.q: What do ribs protect?
questions.a: The heart and lungs.

days.guide: Build a paper skeleton with brad joints; label 6 bones.

questions.q: What is a joint?
questions.a: A place where two bones meet so the body can bend.

days.guide: Feel the biceps when bending the arm and triceps when straightening.

questions.q: Which muscle bends your elbow?
questions.a: Biceps.

questions.q: Which straightens it?
questions.a: Triceps.

days.guide: Teach that calcium (milk, yogurt, cheese, leafy greens) and exercise build strong bones.

questions.q: Name a food with calcium.
questions.a: Milk, yogurt, cheese, broccoli, kale.

days.guide: Label bones; explain how muscles and bones work together.

questions.q: How do muscles move bones?
questions.a: They pull on bones at joints.

weeks.assessment_key: Labeled skeleton (6 bones, e.g.): skull - protects the brain; ribs - protect heart and lungs; spine/backbone - holds you up and protects the spinal cord; pelvis/hip; femur (thigh bone, longest bone); humerus (upper arm). Explanation: muscles attach to bones and pull them to move at joints. Proficient = 6 correct labels + explanation.

weeks.prep: Tennis ball; plastic bottle, balloons, straw, rubber band, scissors (adult cuts) for a lung model; timer.
misconceptions: Thinking lungs are hollow balloons: they are spongy organs full of tiny air sacs.
Thinking the heart is shaped like a valentine: it's a fist-sized muscle.

days.guide: Squeeze a tennis ball hard; the heart squeezes like this all day to pump blood.

questions.q: About how big is your heart?
questions.a: About the size of your fist.

questions.q: What does the heart pump?
questions.a: Blood.

days.guide: Build a balloon lung model in a bottle; pull the bottom balloon to inflate the inside one.

questions.q: What does the bottom balloon model?
questions.a: The diaphragm (muscle under the lungs).

questions.q: What happens when you pull it down?
questions.a: Air rushes in and the 'lung' balloon fills.

days.guide: Count breaths per minute at rest and after jumping.

questions.q: Why do you breathe faster after jumping?
questions.a: Your muscles need more oxygen.

days.guide: List ways to keep heart and lungs healthy.

questions.q: Name two ways.
questions.a: Exercise, eat healthy, never smoke or vape, avoid secondhand smoke.

days.guide: Explain how heart and lungs work together.

questions.q: What is oxygen?
questions.a: A gas in the air your body needs to live.

weeks.assessment_key: Oral explanation: lungs breathe in air with oxygen; oxygen passes into the blood; the heart pumps oxygen-rich blood to the body; blood brings carbon dioxide back to the lungs to breathe out. Proficient = mentions lungs taking in oxygen, heart pumping blood, oxygen delivered to the body.

weeks.prep: Zip-top bag, crackers, water (a little orange juice optional), a clean stocking or knee-high, scissors, tray.
misconceptions: Thinking food goes straight from mouth to stomach without a tube: the esophagus carries it.
Thinking the stomach does all digestion: most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine.

days.guide: Teach the path: mouth, esophagus, stomach, small and large intestines.

questions.q: What carries food from the mouth to the stomach?
questions.a: The esophagus.

days.guide: Mash crackers and water in a zip bag like the stomach.

questions.q: What does the stomach do?
questions.a: Squeezes and mixes food with digestive juices into mush.

days.guide: Squeeze the mush through a stocking like the intestines.

questions.q: What does the small intestine do?
questions.a: Absorbs nutrients into the blood.

days.guide: Discuss fiber and water helping digestion.

questions.q: Why are fiber and water important?
questions.a: They help food move smoothly through your intestines.

days.guide: Draw and label the digestive system.

questions.q: What is digestion?
questions.a: Breaking food down so the body can use its nutrients.

weeks.assessment_key: Labeled diagram: mouth (teeth chew, saliva) → esophagus (tube to stomach) → stomach (mashes and mixes with juices) → small intestine (absorbs nutrients into blood) → large intestine (absorbs water, forms waste). Proficient = 5 parts in order with jobs.

weeks.prep: Mystery bags (cotton ball, sandpaper, spoon), blindfold, small foods to taste and smell (check allergies), eye chart printout.
misconceptions: Thinking the eyes or ears 'see' or 'hear' alone: the brain interprets their messages.
Putting small objects in ears to clean them: never put anything in ears.

days.guide: Blindfolded touch, smell and taste stations.

questions.q: What are the five senses?
questions.a: Sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch.

days.guide: Teach that sense organs send messages through nerves to the brain.

questions.q: What carries messages to the brain?
questions.a: Nerves.

days.guide: Do a simple eye chart and whisper test; explain checkups.

questions.q: Why get vision and hearing checks?
questions.a: To catch problems early so you can see and hear well.

days.guide: List ways to protect each sense organ.

questions.q: How do you protect your skin?
questions.a: Sunscreen, protective clothing, gloves.

days.guide: Match each sense to its organ and a protection tip.

questions.q: Which organ is for smell?
questions.a: Nose.

weeks.assessment_key: Matching: eyes - sight - wear sunglasses/goggles; ears - hearing - keep volume low; nose - smell - avoid sniffing chemicals; tongue - taste - don't taste unknown substances / avoid very hot foods; skin - touch - sunscreen, gloves. Proficient = 5/5 senses with tips.

weeks.prep: Baby photo, measuring tape, paper for a timeline.
misconceptions: Thinking everyone should be the same size at the same age: kids grow at different rates.
Thinking older adults don't have needs: every life stage has needs.

days.guide: Compare a baby photo to now; list new abilities.

questions.q: What can you do now that you couldn't as a baby?
questions.a: Walk, talk, read, ride a bike.

days.guide: Measure height, hand span, foot; compare with family.

questions.q: Who is tallest in your family?
questions.a: Answer from measurements.

days.guide: Make a life-stage timeline with needs.

questions.q: Put in order: teen, infant, adult, child.
questions.a: Infant, child, teen, adult.

days.guide: Discuss how kids grow at different rates.

questions.q: Is it normal to be shorter or taller than a friend?
questions.a: Yes, everyone grows at their own rate.

days.guide: Present the timeline and one way you've grown.

questions.q: What does unique mean?
questions.a: One of a kind.

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline: infant, toddler, child, teen, adult, older adult in order, each with a need (infant - feeding, diapers, care; toddler - safety, play; child - learning, healthy food; teen - independence, guidance; adult - work, caring for family; older adult - health care, help, company). Presentation names one way they've grown. Proficient = 6 stages in order with needs.

weeks.prep: Bike, helmet, chalk; a safe crosswalk; your car's booster seat.
misconceptions: Looking only one way before crossing: look left, right, then left again.
Wearing a helmet tipped back: it should sit level, two fingers above eyebrows.

days.guide: At a crosswalk with a parent: stop, look left-right-left, listen, cross.

questions.q: Why look left again?
questions.a: Cars in the nearest lane come from the left, and things can change quickly.

questions.q: What is a pedestrian?
questions.a: A person walking.

days.guide: Check helmet fit with 2-V-1.

questions.q: What is the 2-V-1 rule?
questions.a: 2 fingers above eyebrows, straps make a V under ears, 1 finger under the chin strap.

days.guide: Practice hand signals and stopping on a chalk course.

questions.q: What is the signal for a left turn?
questions.a: Left arm straight out to the side.

questions.q: For stop?
questions.a: Left arm bent down at the elbow, palm back.

days.guide: Learn why kids ride in boosters in the back seat with seat belts. California law: children under 8 ride in a car seat or booster in the back seat (unless 4'9" or taller).

questions.q: Where is the safest place for kids to ride?
questions.a: In the back seat, buckled in a booster or car seat.

questions.q: Why use a booster?
questions.a: It lifts you so the seat belt fits across your chest and hips, not your neck and belly.

days.guide: Demonstrate crosswalk safety and helmet fit.

questions.q: Where should you cross the street?
questions.a: At a crosswalk or corner, with an adult.

weeks.assessment_key: Demonstration checklist: crosswalk - stops at curb, looks left-right-left, listens, crosses with an adult, keeps looking. Helmet 2-V-1: two fingers above eyebrows, straps form a V under each ear, one finger fits under the buckled chin strap. Proficient = all steps.

weeks.prep: A life jacket (or picture), scenario cards, sunscreen; access to a playground.
misconceptions: Thinking strong swimmers can swim alone: always swim with an adult watching.
Jumping in to save someone: reach or throw, don't go.

days.guide: At a playground, identify safe and unsafe behaviors.

questions.q: Name a safe slide rule.
questions.a: One at a time, feet first, sitting down.

days.guide: Teach: swim with an adult, wear a life jacket, never swim alone.

questions.q: When should you wear a life jacket?
questions.a: On boats and in open water, and whenever you aren't a strong swimmer.

questions.q: What does a lifeguard do?
questions.a: Watches swimmers and helps in emergencies.

days.guide: Practice 'reach or throw, don't go' with a towel or a floating object.

questions.q: What should you do if someone is struggling in water?
questions.a: Shout for an adult; reach with a pole/towel or throw something that floats; don't go in.

days.guide: Review sun safety and overheating signs (very sweaty, dizzy, headache, sick to stomach, very tired).

questions.q: What should you do if you feel too hot and dizzy?
questions.a: Stop, go to shade, drink water, tell an adult.

days.guide: Sort scenarios into safe and unsafe.

questions.q: Is running near the pool safe?
questions.a: No, you could slip and fall.

weeks.assessment_key: Scenario sort (examples): safe - swimming with a lifeguard/adult watching, wearing a life jacket on a boat, sliding feet first, drinking water and resting in shade on a hot day; unsafe - swimming alone, pushing on the slide, jumping in to save a friend, running by the pool, playing hard in the heat without water. Proficient = all correct.

weeks.prep: Smoke alarm (test with a parent), paper for an escape map.
misconceptions: Hiding from fire under a bed or in a closet: get out and stay out.
Going back in for a pet or toy: never go back inside; tell firefighters.

days.guide: Teach smoke alarms; test one with a parent (test monthly).

questions.q: What does a smoke alarm do?
questions.a: Beeps loudly to warn you of smoke or fire.

questions.q: How often should alarms be tested?
questions.a: Once a month.

days.guide: Practice stop, drop, roll and crawling low under smoke.

questions.q: When do you stop, drop and roll?
questions.a: If your clothes catch fire.

questions.q: Why crawl low?
questions.a: Cleaner air is near the floor; smoke rises.

days.guide: Draw an escape map with two ways out of each room.

questions.q: Why two ways out?
questions.a: In case one way is blocked by fire or smoke.

days.guide: Family fire drill to the meeting place.

questions.q: Where do you go after getting out?
questions.a: To the family meeting place outside.

days.guide: Explain your escape plan and fire rules.

questions.q: Should you go back for a toy?
questions.a: No, never go back inside.

weeks.assessment_key: Escape map: each room shows two ways out (door and window), and an outside meeting place is marked. Rules: get low and go under smoke, feel the door with the back of the hand (if hot, use the other way), stop-drop-roll if clothes catch fire, never go back in, call 911 from outside. Proficient = map complete + 4 rules.

weeks.prep: Backpack, flashlight, water bottles, first-aid items, snacks for an emergency kit; paper with your address and phone number.
misconceptions: Running outside during shaking: drop, cover and hold on until shaking stops.
Calling 911 for small problems or as a joke: only for real emergencies.

days.guide: Teach and practice drop, cover, hold on in several rooms.

questions.q: What are the three steps?
questions.a: Drop to hands and knees, cover your head and neck (under a table), hold on.

questions.q: What if there is no table?
questions.a: Get down next to an inside wall, cover your head and neck with your arms.

days.guide: Help build a family emergency kit.

questions.q: Name 3 items for an emergency kit.
questions.a: Water, food, flashlight, batteries, first-aid kit, medicines, blanket.

days.guide: Role-play a 911 call: name, address, emergency; stay on the line.

questions.q: When should you call 911?
questions.a: In an emergency: fire, someone badly hurt or not waking up, danger.

questions.q: What do you tell the operator?
questions.a: Your name, address, and what is happening; stay on the line.

days.guide: Memorize address and a parent's phone number.

questions.q: Say your address.
questions.a: Child recites correctly.

days.guide: Surprise drill; recite address and phone number.

questions.q: When can you stop holding on?
questions.a: When the shaking stops.

weeks.assessment_key: Drill: drops to hands and knees, covers head/neck under a sturdy table, holds on until shaking stops, in any room. Memorization: recites full home address (number, street, city) and a parent's phone number correctly. Proficient = correct drill + accurate recall.

weeks.prep: Scenario cards you write in advance. PARENTAL PREVIEW: read this week first. Use correct, calm language; reassure your child that they will never be in trouble for telling you about a touch, secret, or person that makes them uncomfortable.
misconceptions: Thinking only strangers can be unsafe: anyone who asks to break body-safety rules is not following rules; tell a trusted adult.
Thinking you must keep every secret: secrets about touching or that make you feel unsafe must always be told.

days.guide: Discuss safe touches (hugs from family, high fives, doctor check with parent present) and unsafe ones; your body belongs to you.

questions.q: Who is the boss of your body?
questions.a: I am.

questions.q: What is a safe touch?
questions.a: A touch that is kind and makes you feel safe, like a hug from family when you want it.

days.guide: Practice saying 'No!' firmly, getting away, and telling a trusted adult.

questions.q: What are the three steps?
questions.a: Say No, Go (get away), Tell a trusted adult.

days.guide: Teach 'tricky people': anyone asking a child for help, offering gifts, or asking you to keep secrets. Never go anywhere without a parent's permission.

questions.q: Should an adult ask a kid for help finding a lost pet?
questions.a: No, adults ask other adults for help; say no and tell.

questions.q: Can you go with someone without asking your parent first?
questions.a: No, always check first.

days.guide: Contrast surprises (fun, told soon, like a birthday gift) with unsafe secrets (make you feel bad, 'never tell').

questions.q: Is a birthday present a secret or a surprise?
questions.a: A surprise; it will be told soon and makes people happy.

questions.q: What do you do with an unsafe secret?
questions.a: Tell a trusted adult right away.

days.guide: Respond to 4 scenarios with No-Go-Tell.

questions.q: Who will you tell?
questions.a: A trusted adult, like a parent.

weeks.assessment_key: Scenario responses using No-Go-Tell (examples): 1) Someone wants to touch you where a swimsuit covers: say 'No!', get away, tell a trusted adult. 2) A person in a car asks you to help find a puppy: say no, go to your grown-up, tell. 3) Someone says 'Don't tell your mom about our secret game': say no, leave, tell. 4) An adult you don't know offers a ride home: say no, go, tell. Proficient = all 4 use No-Go-Tell and child names a trusted adult.

weeks.prep: Computer or tablet; scenario cards. PARENTAL PREVIEW: keep weapon talk simple and calm; check that any firearms in your home are stored locked and unloaded.
misconceptions: Thinking a toy-looking gun is safe to touch: never touch; you can't tell if it's real or loaded.
Thinking online friends are real friends: you can't be sure who someone is online.

days.guide: Teach private information: full name, address, school, phone number, photos.

questions.q: Is it okay to tell someone online your address?
questions.a: No, keep it private.

days.guide: Make family online rules: ask first, tell an adult about anything uncomfortable.

questions.q: What do you do if a message makes you uncomfortable?
questions.a: Stop, don't answer, tell a trusted adult.

days.guide: Teach: if you see a gun, don't touch, leave the area, tell an adult.

questions.q: What do you do if you find a gun?
questions.a: Don't touch it, leave the area, tell an adult right away.

days.guide: Role-play online messages and finding a weapon.

questions.q: Someone online asks for your photo. What do you do?
questions.a: Say no, don't send it, tell a parent.

days.guide: Give the safety unit quiz.

questions.q: What is personal information?
questions.a: Facts about you that could help someone find you, like your address or school.

weeks.assessment_key: Safety quiz (weeks 24-29, sample): 1) Look left-right-left before crossing. 2) Helmet 2-V-1. 3) Kids ride in the back seat in a booster. 4) Never swim alone; reach or throw, don't go. 5) Stop, drop, roll; crawl low; two ways out; meeting place. 6) Drop, cover, hold on. 7) 911: name, address, emergency. 8) No-Go-Tell. 9) Keep name, address, school and photos private online; tell an adult about uncomfortable messages. 10) If you see a gun: don't touch, leave the area, tell an adult. Proficient = 8/10.

weeks.prep: An empty medicine box and label (with a parent). PARENTAL PREVIEW: keep all real medicines locked up during this week.
misconceptions: Thinking medicine is candy: never take medicine unless a trusted adult gives it.
Thinking more medicine works better: the right dose is important; too much can hurt.

days.guide: Teach: medicines help when used correctly; drugs used the wrong way can harm.

questions.q: What is a medicine?
questions.a: Something that helps the body when you are sick or hurt, used the right way.

questions.q: What is a prescription?
questions.a: Medicine a doctor orders for one person.

days.guide: Look at a label with a parent; find dose and warnings.

questions.q: What is a dose?
questions.a: How much medicine to take and when.

days.guide: Discuss why only trusted adults give medicine.

questions.q: Who can give you medicine?
questions.a: A parent or trusted adult, doctor or nurse.

days.guide: Compare look-alike candies and pills (pictures).

questions.q: If you find a pill that looks like candy, what do you do?
questions.a: Don't eat it; give it to or tell an adult.

days.guide: Explain 3 medicine safety rules.

questions.q: Can you take your friend's medicine?
questions.a: No, never take someone else's medicine.

weeks.assessment_key: Three rules (any 3 accurate): only take medicine from a trusted adult (parent, doctor, nurse); never take someone else's medicine; follow the label's dose; never guess if something is candy or medicine; keep medicine stored away. Proficient = 3 accurate rules with reasons.

weeks.prep: Household product labels (with a parent), stickers; phone to save the Poison Control number.
misconceptions: Thinking bright bottles are juice: never taste anything unknown.
Trying to make someone throw up: call Poison Control right away.

days.guide: Find warning labels and the poison symbol with a parent.

questions.q: What do warning words like 'Caution' and 'Danger' mean?
questions.a: The product can hurt you; don't touch or taste.

days.guide: Check that cleaners are stored up high or locked.

questions.q: Why store cleaners up high or locked?
questions.a: So young children can't reach them.

days.guide: Learn Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222; save it in the phone.

questions.q: What is the Poison Control number?

days.guide: Practice saying no to tasting unknown substances.

questions.q: What do you say if someone offers you something unknown to taste?
questions.a: 'No, thanks,' and tell an adult.

days.guide: Identify 5 dangerous products; explain what to do if swallowed.

questions.q: Someone swallows a cleaner. What happens next?
questions.a: Tell an adult right away; call Poison Control (or 911 if they are not breathing or won't wake up).

weeks.assessment_key: Identification: names 5 dangerous products (e.g., bleach, drain cleaner, dishwasher detergent pods, laundry pods, bug spray, medicine, car fluids like antifreeze). What to do: tell an adult right away; adult calls Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (or 911 if the person is unconscious or can't breathe). Proficient = 5 products + correct steps.

weeks.prep: Two sponges (one clean, one darkened with brown paint or coffee to model smoke damage), paper and markers. PARENTAL PREVIEW: discuss calmly; avoid shaming family members who smoke.
misconceptions: Thinking vaping is safe or 'just water': vapes contain nicotine and chemicals that harm lungs.
Thinking secondhand smoke doesn't matter: breathing others' smoke harms health too.

days.guide: Teach how tobacco and vaping harm lungs, heart and teeth; nicotine is addictive.

questions.q: Name a harm of smoking or vaping.
questions.a: Damages lungs, hurts the heart, stains teeth, causes bad breath.

questions.q: What does addictive mean?
questions.a: Hard to stop once you start.

days.guide: Compare a clean sponge and a dark, gunky sponge; discuss secondhand smoke.

questions.q: What is secondhand smoke?
questions.a: Smoke breathed in by people near someone who is smoking.

days.guide: Discuss how friends, family and ads influence choices.

questions.q: How might ads make vaping look?
questions.a: Cool, fun, flavored; they hide the harm.

days.guide: Practice refusal: say no, give a reason, walk away.

questions.q: What are the refusal steps?
questions.a: Say no, give a reason, walk away.

days.guide: Make a 'Smoke-Free Me' poster; role-play refusal.

questions.q: Why is alcohol unsafe for kids?
questions.a: It harms a growing brain and body and affects thinking and balance.

weeks.assessment_key: Poster: clear smoke-free message with at least 2 accurate harms (damages lungs, makes it hard to breathe, harms heart, stains teeth, bad breath, nicotine is addictive). Refusal role-play: says 'No,' gives a reason ('it hurts my lungs'), walks away or changes the subject. Proficient = all.

weeks.prep: 'Community Helpers' library books; questions for an interview; card paper.
misconceptions: Thinking only doctors help health: nurses, dentists, pharmacists and public health workers do too.
Fearing checkups: checkups keep you healthy and find problems early.

days.guide: Learn about doctors, nurses, dentists, pharmacists and school nurses.

questions.q: What does a pharmacist do?
questions.a: Prepares medicines and explains how to take them safely.

days.guide: Interview a health helper or family member about their job.

questions.q: What question did you ask?
questions.a: Records question and answer.

days.guide: Learn what happens at a checkup and why vaccines matter.

questions.q: What happens at a checkup?
questions.a: Measure height and weight, listen to heart and lungs, check eyes, ears, and give vaccines if needed.

questions.q: Why do vaccines matter?
questions.a: They protect you and others from serious diseases.

days.guide: Write a thank-you card to a health helper.

questions.q: Why thank health helpers?
questions.a: They work to keep us healthy and safe.

days.guide: Match 6 helpers to their jobs.

questions.q: Who cares for your teeth?
questions.a: A dentist.

weeks.assessment_key: Matching: doctor - checks health and treats illness; nurse - cares for patients, gives shots, checks vital signs; dentist - cares for teeth; pharmacist - prepares medicine and explains how to take it; school nurse - helps students who are sick or hurt at school; public health worker - protects the health of a whole community (vaccines, clean water, tracking disease). Interview notes record 3 answers. Proficient = 6/6 + notes.

weeks.prep: Recycling bins, trash bag, gloves, recyclables for a craft.
misconceptions: Thinking recycling is the only 'R': reducing and reusing come first.
Picking up sharp or unknown litter: wear gloves; adults handle sharp objects.

days.guide: Sort household items into reduce, reuse, recycle, trash.

questions.q: What's the difference between reuse and recycle?
questions.a: Reuse: use again as it is; recycle: make into something new.

days.guide: Discuss how pollution affects health.

questions.q: How can air pollution affect people?
questions.a: It can make breathing harder and cause coughing or asthma.

days.guide: Do a cleanup with gloves and an adult.

questions.q: Why wear gloves?
questions.a: To protect hands from germs and sharp things.

days.guide: Make something useful from recyclables.

questions.q: What did you make?
questions.a: Describes project.

days.guide: Explain how a clean environment helps health.

questions.q: What is pollution?
questions.a: Harmful waste in air, water or land.

weeks.assessment_key: Cleanup reflection: describes what was collected and explains that a clean environment keeps air and water clean, prevents injuries and germs, and helps people stay healthy. Three Rs sort correct (reduce = use less, e.g., reusable bottle; reuse = use again, e.g., jar as pencil cup; recycle = paper, cans, plastic bottles). Proficient = all.

weeks.prep: Poster paper, markers, or a device to record a short video.
misconceptions: Making a message too long: one clear message works best.
Forgetting the audience: think about who will see it.

days.guide: Choose a health topic from this year.

questions.q: What does advocate mean?
questions.a: To speak up to help others make healthy choices.

days.guide: Plan a poster or short video.

questions.q: Who is your audience?
questions.a: Names audience.

days.guide: Create the poster or video.

questions.q: What fact supports your message?
questions.a: Accurate fact.

days.guide: Share with family or neighbors.

questions.q: How did people respond?
questions.a: Child reports.

days.guide: Explain why your message matters.

questions.q: Why does your message matter?
questions.a: Explains health benefit.
